考試官左中允戴　批〔溫雅得旨。〕

詩人與淑女之德克配乎君子焉。蓋和敬，閨門之全德也；淑女有焉，其斯以為君子之善偶乎！詩人託興以美后妃者，意謂：人倫莫先於妃匹，而人道惟在於和敬，吾茲於雎鳩而有感焉。雄鳴於前而雌則應之，關關然於水中之洲，其並遊者，若見其情之至而又未常狎也；雌鳴於後而雄則倡之，關關然於河洲之上，其定偶者，若見其類之別而又未甞離也。吾故觀雎鳩而知物之有善偶也。况我淑女，窈然其幽深，而情欲之感無所動於中；窕然其閑雅，而宴私之意無所形於外。徽柔如君子，而以窈窕者承之，則雍雍乎其和者，其情固足以相親也；蓋和勝或近於嫚，而淑女則無之矣。懿恭如君子，而以窈窕者承之，則肅肅乎其敬者，其禮又足以相別也；蓋敬勝或近於離，而淑女則無之矣。吾不圖君
translation_en:
…〔in a nuanced and solemn [?] manner, skillfully embodying the palace women's admiration for virtue.〕
Examiner Chen, Right Admonisher (You zanshan), comments: 〔Composed and leisurely, worthy of recitation.〕
Examiner Dai, Left Companion (Zuo zhongyun), comments: 〔Gentle and refined, capturing the essential meaning.〕

The poet commends the virtuous maiden's virtue for being a worthy match for the lord. Indeed, harmony and reverence constitute the complete virtue of the inner quarters; since the virtuous maiden possesses them, is it not because of this that she makes a fine mate for the lord? The poet uses an evocative image to praise the queen consort, meaning to say: Among human relationships none comes before that of husband and wife, and the way of humanity lies solely in harmony and reverence; here I am moved at the sight of the ospreys. The male calls out in front and the female answers him, crying "guan-guan" on the islet in the water; as they roam together, one seems to see the utmost depth of their affection, yet they are never overly familiar. The female calls out behind and the male leads her, crying "guan-guan" upon the river islet; as fixed mates, one seems to see the distinction between their kind, yet they are never apart. Therefore, by observing the ospreys, I know that creatures have fine mates. How much more so our virtuous maiden: secluded in her deep reserve, no stirrings of passion or desire move within her; graceful in her poised elegance, no hint of idle intimacy appears on the outside. To a lord of such admirable gentleness, when she attends him with her secluded and graceful virtue, how harmonious is their concord—their affection is truly sufficient to bring them close; for an excess of harmony might border on disrespect, yet the virtuous maiden has none of that. To a lord of such admirable reverence, when she attends him with her secluded and graceful virtue, how solemn is their respect—their propriety is moreover sufficient to maintain due distinction between them; for an excess of reverence might border on estrangement, yet the virtuous maiden has none of that. I had not expected that our lord…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子而得斯淑女也吾又不圖淑女而得配君子
也豈非好逑也哉然則方未得而思之切及既
得而樂之深者吾自不容已矣抑於是而知王
化之所由始也君之與后猶陽之與陰相須而
後成者陰陽必和而後生意暢又必陰陽順序
而後和故和敬者所以闡陰陽之秘而理萬物
之宜者也和敬始於閨門而達之於朝廷於邦
國於天下而禮樂可興矣故曰有關雎之意然
後可以行周官之法度信矣哉
視民不恌君子是則是傚
吳三畏
===
同考試官教諭林　批　發周王體教之意宛
然如見且格高詞雅傑作也
同考試官教諭汪　批　體認眞切措詞古雅
乃文之有關世教者宜録
同考試官教諭鄧　批　隹賓身教之意發揮
透徹古雅可以式多士矣允宜于録
同考試官教諭王　批　莊重典雅老成之作
punctuated:
子而得斯淑女也，吾又不圖淑女而得配君子也，豈非好逑也哉！然則方未得而思之切，及既得而樂之深者，吾自不容已矣。抑於是而知王化之所由始也。君之與后，猶陽之與陰，相須而後成者。陰陽必和而後生意暢，又必陰陽順序而後和。故和敬者，所以闡陰陽之秘而理萬物之宜者也。和敬始於閨門，而達之於朝廷、於邦國、於天下，而禮樂可興矣。故曰：「有《關雎》之意，然後可以行《周官》之法度。」信矣哉！

「視民不恌，君子是則是傚。」
吳三畏
同考試官教諭林　批：發周王體教之意，宛然如見，且格高詞雅，傑作也。
同考試官教諭汪　批：體認眞切，措詞古雅，乃文之有關世教者，宜録。
同考試官教諭鄧　批：隹賓身教之意，發揮透徹，古雅可以式多士矣，允宜于録。
同考試官教諭王　批：莊重典雅，老成之作
translation_en:
… that the lord should obtain this virtuous maiden, and I also did not expect that the virtuous maiden should come to match the lord—is she not indeed a good mate! Thus, yearning so earnestly when she was not yet won, and rejoicing so deeply once she was won, are feelings I naturally could not help. Moreover, from this we know where the kingly transformation begins. The ruler and the queen are like yang and yin, which depend on each other to reach completion. Yin and yang must be in harmony before generative vitality can flourish, and yin and yang must follow their proper order before they can be in harmony. Therefore, harmony and reverence are the means by which the mysteries of yin and yang are elucidated and the appropriateness of the myriad things is ordered. When harmony and reverence begin within the inner quarters and extend to the court, to the states, and to all under heaven, rites and music may then be raised up. Hence it is said: "Only when one has the spirit of the 'Guanju' can one carry out the institutions of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan)." Truly so indeed!

"Showing the people not to be frivolous; the gentlemen take them as patterns and imitate them." [Classic of Poetry, "Luming"]
Wu Sanwei 吳三畏
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Lin 林 comments: It brings out the Zhou king's intent of embodying moral instruction as vividly as if seen before one's eyes; furthermore, its style is lofty and its diction refined—a masterpiece.
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Wang 汪 comments: The comprehension is genuine and keen, and the phrasing is archaic and refined. This is a composition relevant to the moral instruction of the age and ought to be recorded.
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Deng 鄧 comments: The meaning of the honored guests teaching by personal example is expounded thoroughly. Its archaic elegance can serve as a model for the many scholars; it is truly fitting to be recorded.
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Wang 王 comments: Dignified and classically refined, the work of a mature hand…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也宜録以式
考試官右賛善陳　批〔意渾詞雅〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔簡潔〕
周王美嘉賔能善乎俗而足法於人焉夫下之
爲俗由上所示也嘉賔之德能使民俗歸厚焉
君子之法之也固宜周王燕饗賔客而美之如
此蓋曰惟民生厚者其性也惟民從上者其習
也惟上無德以示乎民則民始有趨於偷薄而
恌焉者耳今我嘉賔之德音既甚明矣夫是以
===
表儀樹而民知所觀自變其澆漓之舊觀感新
而民知所向自返乎淳朴之真示之以篤人倫
而凡率履於下者皆去其僞以從乎誠也示之
以敦物軌而凡服習於下者皆去其華以從乎
質也蓋自我有嘉賔而民之偷薄者遠矣凡爾
君子同居長民之位者也位同則德不容於或
異同有道民之責者也責同則化不可以或殊
固當則而象之以其所以自治者而治吾身焉
使德之孔昭者亦如嘉賔之足示乎民也效而
punctuated:
也，宜録以式。
考試官右賛善陳批：〔意渾詞雅。〕
考試官左中允戴批：〔簡潔。〕
周王美嘉賔能善乎俗，而足法於人焉。夫下之爲俗，由上所示也。嘉賔之德，能使民俗歸厚焉，君子之法之也固宜。周王燕饗賔客而美之如此，蓋曰：惟民生厚者，其性也；惟民從上者，其習也。惟上無德以示乎民，則民始有趨於偷薄而恌焉者耳。今我嘉賔之德音既甚明矣，夫是以表儀樹而民知所觀，自變其澆漓之舊；觀感新而民知所向，自返乎淳朴之真。示之以篤人倫，而凡率履於下者，皆去其僞以從乎誠也；示之以敦物軌，而凡服習於下者，皆去其華以從乎質也。蓋自我有嘉賔，而民之偷薄者遠矣。凡爾君子，同居長民之位者也，位同則德不容於或異；同有道民之責者也，責同則化不可以或殊。固當則而象之，以其所以自治者而治吾身焉，使德之孔昭者，亦如嘉賔之足示乎民也；效而
translation_en:
… Indeed it should be recorded to serve as a model.
Examiner and Right Admonisher Chen comments: [The thought is profound and the diction elegant.]
Examiner and Left Companion Dai comments: [Concise and clear.]
The King of Zhou praises his worthy guests for being able to improve customs and for being worthy of emulation by others. Now, the customs practiced by those below stem from what is demonstrated by those above. Since the virtue of the worthy guests can cause the customs of the people to return to generosity, it is certainly fitting that the noble men take them as a model. When the King of Zhou feasted his guests and praised them in this manner, he was in effect saying: That the people are born with a generous disposition is their innate nature; that the people follow their superiors is their acquired habit. Only when superiors lack the virtue to demonstrate to the people do the people begin to incline toward frivolity and meanness. Now the virtuous reputation of my worthy guests is already exceedingly bright. Therefore, a standard of conduct is established and the people know what to look up to, naturally transforming their old ways of thinness andperfidy; their inspiration is renewed and the people know in which direction to turn, naturally returning to the genuineness of simplicity and honesty. When shown how to be devoted to human relationships, all who follow and practice below cast aside their falseness to follow sincerity; when shown how to esteem the proper norms of things, all who submit and accustom themselves below cast aside their ostentation to follow substance. Indeed, since I have had these worthy guests, frivolity and meanness among the people have been kept far away. All you noble men occupy alike the positions of rulers over the people; since your positions are the same, your virtue must not be allowed to differ. You share alike the responsibility of guiding the people; since your responsibilities are the same, your transformative influence must not vary. You ought certainly to take them as a rule and pattern, governing your own persons by the means through which they govern themselves, so that the great brightness of your virtue is likewise sufficient, like that of the worthy guests, to be demonstrated to the people; imitating and…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
法之以其所以感人者而感吾民焉使俗之不
恌者亦如民之觀化於嘉賓也夫然則不惟下
之民俗以定而上之士範亦端嘉賓之所以示
我者豈在言語之末哉抑於是而知周之治非
尚文也鹿鳴之燕宴饗求大道也而要其歸惟
曰示民不恌天保之祝多福頌盛德也而極其
化惟曰民之質矣然則尚文豈周家意哉蓋至
於文尚成而大道隱至德微矣讀詩者其尚知
所戒焉
===
春秋
三月作丘甲〔成公元年〕二月辛巳立武宮〔成公六年〕
同考試官教諭伍　批〔平正之格春容之詞〕
程懋德
〔且體認兵制廟制更清切經義之優者可以式〕
矣
考試官右賛善陳　批〔辭義嚴整〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔得謹嚴體〕
punctuated:
法之，以其所以感人者而感吾民焉，使俗之不恌者，亦如民之觀化於嘉賓也。夫然，則不惟下之民俗以定，而上之士範亦端。嘉賓之所以示我者，豈在言語之末哉？抑於是而知周之治非尚文也。《鹿鳴》之燕，宴饗求大道也，而要其歸，惟曰「示民不恌」；《天保》之祝，多福頌盛德也，而極其化，惟曰「民之質矣」。然則尚文豈周家意哉？蓋至於文尚成，而大道隱、至德微矣。讀《詩》者，其尚知所戒焉。

《春秋》
「三月作丘甲」〔成公元年〕，「二月辛巳立武宮」〔成公六年〕。
程懋德
同考試官教諭伍　批：〔平正之格，春容之詞，且體認兵制、廟制更清切，經義之優者，可以式〕矣。
考試官右賛善陳　批：〔辭義嚴整。〕
考試官左中允戴　批：〔得謹嚴體。〕
translation_en:
…and emulate them, using that by which they move others to move our own people, so that the unfrivolous customs will also be like the people observing and being transformed by the honored guests. When it is thus, not only are the customs of the common people below settled, but the model set by the gentlemen above is also made upright. How could that which the honored guests show to us lie merely in the superficialities of words and speech?

Moreover, from this we know that the governance of the Zhou did not prize outward ornament. The feast in the ode "Deer Cry" (Luming) seeks the Great Way through banqueting, yet when summing up its ultimate aim, it simply says, "showing the people not to be frivolous." The blessings in the ode "Heaven Protects" (Tianbao) praise flourishing virtue with abundant fortune, yet when reaching the pinnacle of its transformative influence, it simply says, "the people are simple and honest." If this is so, how could prizing outward ornament have been the intention of the House of Zhou? Indeed, once a preference for outward ornament became established, the Great Way was obscured and supreme virtue grew faint. May those who read the Odes (Shi) take warning from this!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
"In the third month, the district armor levy was instituted" [First year of Duke Cheng]; "In the second month, on the xinsi day, the Palace of Duke Wu was erected" [Sixth year of Duke Cheng].

By Cheng Maode 程懋德.
Associate Examiner Instructor Wu 伍 comments: [A balanced and proper structure with composed and graceful diction; moreover, its grasp of the military system and ancestral temple system is especially clear and incisive. An outstanding essay on the meaning of the Classics that] can serve as a model.
Examiner Right Admonisher Chen 陳 comments: [The diction and meaning are rigorous and well-ordered.]
Examiner Left Companion Dai 戴 comments: [It attains a scrupulous and austere style.]

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
春秋紀望國之戎祀而困民越禮之罪見矣夫
戎祀國之大事也丘甲作則民困武宮立則禮
越春秋皆譏之也宜哉且國之立也以衛民者
莫大乎戎以孝先者莫大乎祀而皆有先王之
禮制存焉者也故大國三軍制也不可加也魯
固大國耳胡乃懼齊難之至而丘甲作焉則新
籍大盈於舊額殊亂乎司馬之法向之一丘十
有八人者今則二十五人矣向之一甸七十二
人者今則百人矣計三甸而增一乘每一乘而
===
增一甲魯之民力能堪耶故春秋特書曰作言
前所無者今不宜作也而困民之罪彰矣諸侯
五廟禮也不可過也魯亦諸侯耳胡乃侈戰㩦
之功而武宮立焉則毁廟更創爲新覩殊紊乎
宗伯之辨以其主則奉祧巳久而今復班於祖
考矣以其祭則去墠巳久而今復列於饗嘗矣
親旣盡而情猶及世旣遠而祀猶隆魯之秉禮
宜爾耶故春秋特書曰立言前所遷者今不宜
立也而越禮之罪昭矣吁聖人之重民而謹禮
punctuated: 《春秋》紀望國之戎祀，而困民越禮之罪見矣。夫戎、祀，國之大事也。丘甲作則民困，武宮立則禮越，《春秋》皆譏之也，宜哉！且國之立也，以衛民者莫大乎戎，以孝先者莫大乎祀，而皆有先王之禮制存焉者也。故大國三軍，制也，不可加也。魯固大國耳，胡乃懼齊難之至而丘甲作焉？則新籍大盈於舊額，殊亂乎司馬之法。向之一丘十有八人者，今則二十五人矣；向之一甸七十二人者，今則百人矣。計三甸而增一乘，每一乘而增一甲，魯之民力能堪耶？故《春秋》特書曰「作」，言前所無者今不宜作也，而困民之罪彰矣。諸侯五廟，禮也，不可過也。魯亦諸侯耳，胡乃侈戰㩦之功而武宮立焉？則毁廟更創爲新覩，殊紊乎宗伯之辨。以其主，則奉祧巳久，而今復班於祖考矣；以其祭，則去墠巳久，而今復列於饗嘗矣。親旣盡而情猶及，世旣遠而祀猶隆，魯之秉禮宜爾耶？故《春秋》特書曰「立」，言前所遷者今不宜立也，而越禮之罪昭矣。吁！聖人之重民而謹禮…
translation_en:
When the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records the military affairs and sacrifices of a prestigious state, the crimes of exhausting the people and transgressing the rites become evident. Now, military affairs and sacrifices are the great affairs of a state. When the district armor levy (qiujia) was instituted, the people were exhausted; when the Shrine of Duke Wu (Wugong) was established, the rites were transgressed. That the Spring and Autumn Annals censures both is fitting indeed!

Moreover, in the founding of a state, for defending the people nothing is greater than military affairs, and for showing filial piety to ancestors nothing is greater than sacrifices; yet in both there exist the ritual institutions of the former kings. Thus, for a great state to have three armies is the institution, which cannot be increased. Lu was indeed merely a great state; why then, fearing the arrival of hostilities from Qi, did it institute the district armor levy? In doing so, the new registers greatly exceeded the old quotas, throwing the laws of the Minister of War (Sima) into utter confusion. Where formerly one district (qiu) supplied eighteen men, now it was twenty-five men; where formerly one tract (dian) supplied seventy-two men, now it was a hundred men. Reckoning an increase of one chariot for every three tracts, and an increase of one armored soldier (jia) for each chariot, how could the strength of the people of Lu bear this? Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals specially recorded it as "instituted" (zuo), meaning that what did not exist before ought not now be instituted—and thus the crime of exhausting the people was made manifest.

For the feudal lords to have five ancestral temples is the rite, which cannot be exceeded. Lu too was merely a feudal lord; why then, boasting of the achievement of victory in battle [?], did it establish the Shrine of Duke Wu? In doing so, a demolished temple was newly erected as a fresh spectacle, throwing the distinctions of the Minister of Rites (Zongbo) into utter disorder. As for his spirit tablet, it had long since been removed to the repository for distant ancestors (tiao), yet now it was once again ranked alongside the immediate ancestors; as for his sacrifices, they had long since departed thecleared-earth altar (shan), yet now they were once again arrayed among the seasonal offerings (xiangchang). When kinship has already been exhausted, yet affection still extends to him; when the generations have already grown distant, yet the sacrifices remain grand—for Lu, which upholds the rites, ought it to be thus? Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals specially recorded it as "established" (li), meaning that what had previously been removed ought not now be established—and thus the crime of transgressing the rites was made clear.

Alas! How the Sage valued the people and was謹 cautious regarding the rites…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也如此哉雖然聖人又有誅其心者在焉季孫
始懼齊人之侮而思益兵以雪耻是憤也既因
齊師之敗而遂廣祀以侈功是驕也驕憤一萌
而下疲民力上違王禮不顧焉然則又將何所
忌憚哉嗚呼此季孫之所以日横而公室愈卑
有由也
六月癸卯晉師滅赤狄潞氏以潞子嬰兒
歸〔宣公十有五年〕春王正月晉人滅赤
狄甲氏及留吁〔宣公十有六年〕八月晉
荀吳帥師滅陸渾之戎〔昭公十有七年〕
===
顧紹芳
同考試官教諭伍　批〔語意渾融深得春秋〕
〔安攘之大旨允宜錄出〕
考試官右賛善陳　批〔意婉而詞峻〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔明暢可錄〕
春秋三紀伯兵而獨於晉華無貶焉此見陸渾
之滅而靖王圻不與滅潞甲之圖闢地等也且
戎狄與中華畫疆而國何代無之然王者馭之
punctuated:
也如此哉！雖然，聖人又有誅其心者在焉。季孫始懼齊人之侮，而思益兵以雪耻，是憤也；既因齊師之敗，而遂廣祀以侈功，是驕也。驕憤一萌，而下疲民力、上違王禮不顧焉，然則又將何所忌憚哉？嗚呼！此季孫之所以日横，而公室愈卑，有由也。

「六月，癸卯，晉師滅赤狄潞氏，以潞子嬰兒歸。」〔宣公十有五年〕「春，王正月，晉人滅赤狄甲氏及留吁。」〔宣公十有六年〕「八月，晉荀吳帥師滅陸渾之戎。」〔昭公十有七年〕

顧紹芳
同考試官教諭伍　批〔語意渾融，深得《春秋》〕〔安攘之大旨，允宜錄出。〕
考試官右賛善陳　批〔意婉而詞峻。〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔明暢可錄。〕

《春秋》三紀伯兵，而獨於晉華無貶焉。此見陸渾之滅而靖王圻，不與滅潞、甲之圖闢地等也。且戎狄與中華畫疆而國，何代無之？然王者馭之
translation_en:
… so deeply did [the Sage value the people and guard the rites]! Even so, the Sage also had that by which he condemned their underlying motives. At first, Jisun feared the insults of the people of Qi and thought of increasing his troops to wipe away the shame—this was resentment. Then, following the defeat of the Qi army, he went on to expand the ancestral sacrifices to boast of his achievement—this was arrogance. Once arrogance and resentment sprouted, he disregarded exhausting the people's strength below and violating the royal rites above; what, then, would he still shrink from doing? Alas! That Jisun grew more overbearing by the day while the ducal house became ever more abased—there was indeed a reason for it.

"In the sixth month, on the day guimao, the army of Jin extinguished the Lushi tribe of the Red Di, and brought back Ying'er, Viscount of Lu." [Duke Xuan, 15th year] "In spring, in the King's first month, the people of Jin extinguished the Jiashi tribe of the Red Di and the Liuxu." [Duke Xuan, 16th year] "In the eighth month, Xun Wu of Jin led an army and extinguished the Rong of Luhun." [Duke Zhao, 17th year]

Gu Shaofang 顧紹芳
Associate Examiner, Instructor Wu 伍 comments: [The wording and meaning are harmoniously integrated, deeply grasping the great purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) regarding pacifying the interior and repelling the exterior; it certainly ought to be selected for publication.]
Examiner, Right Admonisher Chen 陳 comments: [The thought is subtle while the diction is incisive.]
Examiner, Left Companion Dai 戴 comments: [Clear and fluent; worthy of being selected.]

The Spring and Autumn Annals three times records the military expeditions of the hegemon, yet only where Jin [cleared the heartland of] China does it withhold censure. From this we see that extinguishing the Luhun to pacify the royal domain is not on a par with extinguishing the Lushi and Jiashi in order to expand territory. Moreover, in what era have the Rong and Di not demarcated borders and established states alongside the central lands of China? Yet the true king's way of controlling them…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有道矣兼覆謂仁彼安土而殄之過也別生謂
義彼亂華而縱之亦過也晉嘗三事于戎狄矣
潞氏之滅也不曰釋娣之憾乎即有召兵之繇
而罪以一人可已矣剪焉而糞除之何遽忍如
是甲氏之滅也不曰遷潞之怒乎始無侵疆之
罪而亡其一族已暴矣忽焉而波及之何太甚
如是夫滅者非以亂華也信滅之者難言靖華
也宜經貶之若陸渾之滅則異是何也陸渾之
雜處伊川而密邇王室豈若潞氏甲氏之列在
===
遠服無煩戒嚴哉地臨象闕而異類與居防其
漬矣人負狼心而圻甸與比禍其釀矣噫若此
者胡可弗圖之是役也討楚之睦而甘鹿奔無
論造意何如自今戎馬不牧于王郊一代剝膚
之患庶其除之也告周以祭而棘津涉無論舉
事何如自今神州不染于戎俗百年胥溺之憂
庶其拯之也彼林父士會以土地故而再勤兵
者可與同日道哉故經于荀吳獨無貶焉或稱
師或稱人或稱名氏而聖人仁義之權衡章章
punctuated: 有道矣。兼覆謂仁，彼安土而殄之，過也；別生謂義，彼亂華而縱之，亦過也。晉嘗三事于戎狄矣。潞氏之滅也，不曰釋娣之憾乎？即有召兵之繇，而罪以一人可已矣，剪焉而糞除之，何遽忍如是！甲氏之滅也，不曰遷潞之怒乎？始無侵疆之罪，而亡其一族已暴矣，忽焉而波及之，何太甚如是！夫滅者非以亂華也，信滅之者難言靖華也，宜經貶之。若陸渾之滅則異是。何也？陸渾之雜處伊川而密邇王室，豈若潞氏、甲氏之列在遠服，無煩戒嚴哉？地臨象闕，而異類與居，防其潰矣；人負狼心，而圻甸與比，禍其釀矣。噫！若此者，胡可弗圖之？是役也，討楚之睦而甘鹿奔，無論造意何如，自今戎馬不牧于王郊，一代剝膚之患，庶其除之也；告周以祭而棘津涉，無論舉事何如，自今神州不染于戎俗，百年胥溺之憂，庶其拯之也。彼林父、士會以土地故而再勤兵者，可與同日道哉？故經于荀吳獨無貶焉。或稱師，或稱人，或稱名氏，而聖人仁義之權衡章章
translation_en:
… possesses a proper way. Universal shelter is called benevolence; if they dwell peacefully in their land and one exterminates them, that is going too far. Distinguishing kinds of beings is called righteousness; if they throw China into disorder and one lets them go unchecked, that too is going too far.

Jin once undertook three campaigns against the Rong and Di. In the destruction of the Lushi, was it not said to be to vent resentment over the younger sister-consort? Even if there was a pretext for summoning troops, punishing a single person would have sufficed; to clip them off and sweep them away like filth—how could one suddenly be so ruthless! In the destruction of the Jiashi, was it not said to be out of anger rolled over from the Lushi? From the beginning they had committed no crime of invading the borders, and to destroy that one clan was already tyrannical; to suddenly let the repercussions spread to them as well—how could one go to such extremes! Now, those who were destroyed were not destroyed for throwing China into disorder, so truly those who destroyed them can hardly claim to have been pacifying China; it is fitting that the Classic censures them.

As for the destruction of Luhun, however, it was different from this. Why? With Luhun living intermingled along the Yi River and in close proximity to the royal house, how could they be compared to the Lushi and Jiashi, who were arrayed in distant zones of submission and required no heightened alert? When the territory overlooks the palace watchtowers and an alien race dwells amidst them, the defenses are breached [reading 潰 for 漬]; when people harbor wolfish hearts and live right alongside the royal domain, disaster is brewing. Alas! Faced with something like this, how could one fail to take measures against it?

In this campaign, punishing their amity with Chu so that they fled at Ganlu—no matter what the underlying motive was, from this point on Rong horses would no longer graze in the royal suburbs, and the skin-flaying affliction of an entire era might thereby be removed. Announcing a sacrifice to Zhou and fording at Jijin—no matter how the enterprise was carried out, from this point on the sacred heartland would no longer be tainted by Rong customs, and the百年 worry of all sinking into ruin together might thereby be relieved. Can those like荀林父 (Xun Linfu) and 士會 (Shi Hui), who twice mobilized troops merely for the sake of territory, be spoken of on the same day as this?

Therefore, the Classic withholds censure from Xun Wu alone. In one case it speaks of "the army," in another of "a man," and in another it names the person and his clan—and the Sage's balance of benevolence and righteousness is brightly…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
著矣雖然陸渾固晉所遷而來也今之討徒楚
故耳豈誠有靖華意哉夫子慨戎索不修而幸
雒無陸渾故于吳特恕之非爲吳也恐後世有
兵舉于靖華而〈〉亦以徼功生事詆訾之也以
此爲坊猶有浸淫爲晉代之事者
禮記
五行以爲質故事可復也
陸起龍
同考試官推官史　批〔聖人法五行以作則〕
其義甚精是作發得明透可以式矣
===
考試官右賛善陳　批〔結構精密〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔醇雅之作〕
聖人法氣運以經政而其用不窮焉蓋終則必
始者五行之運也事正於此而皆可復矣夫焉
有所窮哉禮運君子若曰聖人之所以率作其
民者事也民之所以作而不倦者事之可復也
而何以得之蓋自陽變陰合而五行出焉本無
往而不復也作則者以之爲質則是玩氣機之
punctuated:
著矣。雖然，陸渾固晉所遷而來也。今之討，徒楚故耳，豈誠有靖華意哉？夫子慨戎索不修，而幸雒無陸渾，故于吳特恕之，非爲吳也，恐後世有兵舉于靖華，而〈〉亦以徼功生事詆訾之也。以此爲坊，猶有浸淫爲晉代之事者。

《禮記》
「五行以爲質，故事可復也。」
陸起龍
同考試官推官史　批：〔聖人法五行以作則，〕其義甚精。是作發得明透，可以式矣。
考試官右賛善陳　批：〔結構精密。〕
考試官左中允戴　批：〔醇雅之作。〕

聖人法氣運以經政，而其用不窮焉。蓋終則必始者，五行之運也；事正於此，而皆可復矣，夫焉有所窮哉？《禮運》君子若曰：聖人之所以率作其民者，事也；民之所以作而不倦者，事之可復也。而何以得之？蓋自陽變陰合而五行出焉，本無往而不復也。作則者以之爲質，則是玩氣機之
translation_en:
…becomes manifest. Even so, the Luhun Rong had originally been relocated there by Jin. Their punitive campaign now was merely on account of Chu; how could they genuinely have had the intention of pacifying the Chinese heartland? The Master lamented that the regulations for the Rong were no longer maintained, yet was glad that the Luo region was rid of the Luhun. Thus he showed special leniency toward [Xun] Wu—not for Wu's sake, but out of fear that in later ages when military action was undertaken to pacify the Chinese heartland, [people] [?] would likewise slander it as seeking merit and stirring up trouble. Even with this set up as a dike, there were still those whose gradual degeneration led to the events of the Jin dynasty.

Record of Rites (Liji)
"Taking the Five Phases as the substantive basis, affairs can therefore be repeated."
Lu Qilong

Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Shi, comments: [The sage models himself on the Five Phases to establish rules;] the meaning of this is most subtle. This essay brings it out with clarity and penetration; it can serve as a model.
Examiner, Right Admonisher Chen, comments: [Structurally precise and tight.]
Examiner, Left Companion Dai, comments: [A pure and elegant composition.]

The sage models himself on the movement of vital forces (qiyun) to order governance, and thus its application is inexhaustible. For that which must begin again whenever it ends is the movement of the Five Phases; when affairs are rectified by this standard, they can all be repeated—how then could there be any exhaustion? In the "Evolution of Rites" (Liyun), the gentleman seems to say: That by which the sage leads his people to action is affairs; that by which the people act without growing weary is the repeatability of affairs. And how is this achieved? Ever since yang transformed and yin united to bring forth the Five Phases, by their fundamental nature there has been no going forth without a return. When he who establishes rules takes them as his substantive basis, he contemplates the…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
代謝而遵爲立政之經乘時令之推遷而率爲
成務之準順而有常者其序也而事從取正焉
亦不敢紊其序矣流而不息者其運也而事皆
就正焉亦不敢悖其運矣如是而何不可復哉
吾知要終所以原始而循環無端嗣後所以承
前而周旋不匱寒暑晝夜運而事與之移要之
皆從其期者也今歲之所就緒固可推之來歲
而復然矣其亦如五行之有常也哉春秋冬夏
交而事隨以禪要之必由其舊者也來歲之所
===
繼興固有仍之今歲而不改矣其亦如五行之
不息也哉可見五行之動天地所不能違也事
之可復聖人所不能易也聖人之善作則如此
夫大抵帝王之政莫大於法天授時齊政皆此
質也然觀圖紀修悖之說疇衍從逆之旨又有
不純任乎天者廼知體天心者盡人謀而已不
然下召上應皆以爲事之可復而又安足恃哉
故曰吾之氣順天地之氣亦順聖人參賛之功
可覩也夫
punctuated:
代謝，而遵爲立政之經；乘時令之推遷，而率爲成務之準。順而有常者，其序也，而事從取正焉，亦不敢紊其序矣；流而不息者，其運也，而事皆就正焉，亦不敢悖其運矣。如是，而何不可復哉？吾知要終所以原始，而循環無端；嗣後所以承前，而周旋不匱。寒暑晝夜運，而事與之移，要之皆從其期者也。今歲之所就緒，固可推之來歲而復然矣，其亦如五行之有常也哉！春秋冬夏交，而事隨以禪，要之必由其舊者也。來歲之所繼興，固有仍之今歲而不改矣，其亦如五行之不息也哉！可見五行之動，天地所不能違也；事之可復，聖人所不能易也。聖人之善作則如此夫！

大抵帝王之政，莫大於法天。授時齊政，皆此質也。然觀圖紀修悖之說、疇衍從逆之旨，又有不純任乎天者。廼知體天心者，盡人謀而已。不然，下召上應，皆以爲事之可復，而又安足恃哉？故曰：「吾之氣順，天地之氣亦順。」聖人參賛之功，可覩也夫！
translation_en:
…succession, and adhere to it as the invariant standard for establishing governance; they ride the shifting of the seasonal ordinances, and follow them as the norm for accomplishing affairs. What is orderly and constant is their sequence; as human affairs take their rectification from this, they too do not dare to disrupt that sequence. What flows without cease is their revolution; as human affairs all come to be rectified by this, they too do not dare to go against that revolution. Being thus, how could they not be repeated? I know that summing up the end is the means to trace back the beginning, revolving in an endless cycle; succeeding behind is the means to carry on what went before, coming full circle without exhaustion. Cold and heat, day and night revolve, and affairs shift along with them; in short, all follow their appointed seasons. What is brought to completion this year can surely be extended to the next year and be so again—is this not just like the constancy of the Five Phases! Spring and autumn, winter and summer alternate, and affairs give way in turn along with them; in short, all must follow their old precedents. What rises in succession next year will surely carry on from this year without alteration—is this not just like the ceaselessness of the Five Phases! Thus it can be seen that the movement of the Five Phases is something even Heaven and Earth cannot violate, and the repeatability of affairs is something even the sages cannot alter. Such is the excellence of the sages in establishing standards!

In general, in the governance of emperors and kings, nothing is greater than modeling oneself on Heaven. Granting the seasons and regulating the seven celestial bodies are both based on this fundamental substance. Yet when we examine the doctrine of cultivation and perversity recorded in the River Chart, and the purport of compliance and defiance expounded in the Nine Categories of the Great Plan, there is also that which is not left purely to Heaven. Thus we know that to embody the mind of Heaven is simply to exhaust human counsel. Otherwise, when actions below summon responses above, if one merely assumes that affairs can always be repeated, how could that be relied upon? Therefore it is said: "When our vital breath is in harmony, the vital breath of Heaven and Earth is also in harmony." Here the achievement of the sages in participating in and assisting the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth may be witnessed indeed!

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
唯有德之君爲能行此明足以見之仁足
以與之
楊繼美
同考試官推官史　批〔體裁整飭詞意渾融〕
結歸重于明尤有見
考試官右賛善陳　批〔義精詞達〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔典雅精切〕
賢君之能公惠以其德之備也夫德所以行乎
惠也明仁兼體而君德備矣於公惠乎何有記
===
者獨表之意曰人君之爲治德所以立其本也
惠所以達其用也祭之有畀固爲惠下之道矣
而其孰能行之惟君之有德者爲能存心天下
而溥以兼利之恩加志窮民而錫以均沾之澤
德意旁流則自上逮下斯不病於屯而不施也
德施宏濟則由近及遠自不患於偏而不舉也
而其德如何盖君之於民無見於惠之當與者
惟其未明也知其當與而不與者惟其未仁也
惟有德則明矣聰明睿知皆由此出而不以一
punctuated:
唯有德之君爲能行此，明足以見之，仁足以與之。

楊繼美

同考試官推官史　批〔體裁整飭，詞意渾融，結歸重于明，尤有見。〕
考試官右賛善陳　批〔義精詞達。〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔典雅精切。〕

賢君之能公惠，以其德之備也。夫德所以行乎惠也，明仁兼體而君德備矣，於公惠乎何有？記者獨表之意曰：人君之爲治，德所以立其本也，惠所以達其用也。祭之有畀，固爲惠下之道矣，而其孰能行之？惟君之有德者，爲能存心天下，而溥以兼利之恩；加志窮民，而錫以均沾之澤。德意旁流，則自上逮下，斯不病於屯而不施也；德施宏濟，則由近及遠，自不患於偏而不舉也。而其德如何？盖君之於民，無見於惠之當與者，惟其未明也；知其當與而不與者，惟其未仁也。惟有德則明矣，聰明睿知皆由此出，而不以一
translation_en:
"Only a ruler who possesses virtue is able to practice this; his clarity of vision is sufficient to perceive it, and his benevolence is sufficient to bestow it." (Book of Rites, "Jitong")

Yang Jimei 楊繼美

Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Shi 史, comments: [The structure is neat and well-ordered, and the diction and ideas are harmoniously blended; the conclusion placing particular emphasis on clarity of vision shows especially fine insight.]
Examiner, Right Admonisher Chen 陳, comments: [The meaning is refined and the expression articulate.]
Examiner, Left Companion Dai 戴, comments: [Elegantly classical and precisely to the point.]

That a worthy ruler is able to impartially bestow favor is because his virtue is complete. Now, virtue is that whereby favor is put into practice. When clarity of vision and benevolence are both embodied, a ruler's virtue is complete—what difficulty, then, is there in impartially bestowing favor?

The sense in which the recorder of the rites singled this out to highlight it is as follows: In a ruler's governance, virtue is that whereby its foundation is established, and favor is that whereby its function is realized. The bestowal of remnants at sacrifices is indeed the way of showing favor to those below, yet who is able to put it into practice? Only a ruler who possesses virtue is able to keep the whole world in his heart and widely extend the grace of universal benefit, and to direct his thoughts toward destitute people and grant them the bounty of evenly shared blessings. When virtuous intentions flow forth on all sides, reaching from above down to those below, there is no longer the defect of hoarding without bestowing; when virtuous largesse brings vast relief, extending from the near to the distant, there is naturally no worry of partiality or failure to carry it out.

And what is this virtue like? In a ruler's relation to the people, if he fails to see that favor ought to be given, it is simply because he is not yet clear-sighted; if he knows that it ought to be given and yet does not give it, it is simply because he is not yet benevolent. Only when he possesses virtue is he clear-sighted: keen hearing, clear sight, and perspicacious wisdom all issue from this, and he does not allow a single…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
毫私意自蔽彼其察於民故眞有若一體者焉
而灼識夫惠之不可重積矣明不足以見之乎
有德則仁矣豈弟慈祥皆胥此具而不以一毫
私意自累彼其軫於民隱眞有若恫瘝者焉而
弗靳於惠之所當下流矣仁不足以與之乎有
明而仁之所欲與者無不決有仁而明之所及
見者無不行惠之逮於下也信惟有德者能之
哉抑此仁智之旨也而要以明爲本蓋民之於
君也遠非聰明懸照則閭閻疾苦不徹九重此
===
屯膏之所以可慮而議貸之令不屢下也然明
豈易言哉堯之欽明舜之文明至矣而愽施濟
衆猶然病之君人者可省也
第貳塲
論
世之所以治安
顧憲成
同考試官教諭蔣　批〔塲中作者類牽引浮詞殊失本旨讀之可厭是篇論君民一體發養〕
punctuated:
毫私意自蔽。彼其察於民故，眞有若一體者焉，而灼識夫惠之不可重積矣，明不足以見之乎？有德則仁矣，豈弟慈祥，皆胥此具，而不以一毫私意自累。彼其軫於民隱，眞有若恫瘝者焉，而弗靳於惠之所當下流矣，仁不足以與之乎？有明而仁之所欲與者無不決，有仁而明之所及見者無不行。惠之逮於下也，信惟有德者能之哉！抑此仁智之旨也，而要以明爲本。蓋民之於君也遠，非聰明懸照，則閭閻疾苦不徹九重，此屯膏之所以可慮，而議貸之令不屢下也。然明豈易言哉？堯之欽明，舜之文明，至矣，而愽施濟衆，猶然病之，君人者可省也。

第貳塲
論
《世之所以治安》
顧憲成
同考試官教諭蔣　批〔塲中作者類牽引浮詞，殊失本旨，讀之可厭。是篇論君民一體，發養〕
translation_en:
… hair's breadth of selfish intent. In his discernment of the people's affairs, he truly regards them as sharing a single body with himself, and thus clearly recognizes that favor must not be hoarded. Is such clarity not sufficient to perceive this? When he possesses virtue, he is benevolent: affability, brotherly ease, and compassionate kindness are all thereby complete in him, unencumbered by even a hair's breadth of selfish intent. In his commiseration for the people's hidden sufferings, he truly feels their pain as if it were his own sickness, and thus is never stingy with the favor that ought to flow downward. Is such benevolence not sufficient to bestow it? With clarity, whatever benevolence wishes to bestow is unfailingly decided upon; with benevolence, whatever clarity manages to perceive is unfailingly put into practice. For favor to reach those below—truly, only one who possesses virtue is capable of this!

Moreover, while this is the essential meaning of benevolence and wisdom, in the final analysis it takes clarity as its foundation. For the people are far removed from the ruler; unless his acute hearing and clear sight shine down from on high, the hardships and sufferings of the common alleys will never penetrate the ninefold walls of the palace. This is why hoarding his bounty is cause for concern, and why decrees deliberating relief are not frequently handed down. Yet how can clarity be easily spoken of? The reverent clarity of Yao and the refined clarity of Shun reached the utmost perfection, and yet even they found it difficult to bestow廣泛 benefits and bring relief to the multitude. Those who rule over others ought to reflect on this!

Second Session
Discourse
"How the World Is Brought to Order and Peace"
By Gu Xiancheng 顧憲成
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Jiang 蔣: 〔Writers in the examination compound generally drag in floating, superficial verbiage, altogether losing the original purport of the topic, so that reading them is tiresome. This essay discusses how ruler and people form a single body, bringing out the idea of nourishing …〕

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
民惟恐不足意極爲透徹且格高調古思玄氣
勁是能力黜虛浮而敦崇大雅者可式
同考試官教授黃　批　以古雅之調發剴切
之思蓋有裨於理道者不徒文之工巳也隹士
隹士
考試官右賛善陳　批　有㦲論有操縱發人君養
民治安之意婉曲詳盡宜錄以式
考試官左中允戴　批　得肯而格自昌大氣更悠
揚
===
人君通天下爲一身也是故爲天下急於爲身
而天下之治成焉天下之於君身其相去亦甚
懸者而何至以急於身也君愛其身而天下之
人亦各自愛其身君養巳而不先養人則彼將
競起而各求所爲養焉而天下之事始紛然矣
夫惟不以民視民而視民猶吾身於是愛身必
先於愛民而養民尤急於養身則天下之民始
無有不得其所者夫然後舉天下之民皆委命
於其君而天下可以晏然而無事然則愛民者
punctuated:
民惟恐不足意，極爲透徹。且格高調古，思玄氣勁，是能力黜虛浮而敦崇大雅者，可式。
同考試官教授黃　批：以古雅之調，發剴切之思，蓋有裨於理道者，不徒文之工巳也。隹士，隹士！
考試官右賛善陳　批：有㦲論，有操縱，發人君養民治安之意，婉曲詳盡，宜錄以式。
考試官左中允戴　批：得肯而格自昌大，氣更悠揚。
人君通天下爲一身也，是故爲天下急於爲身，而天下之治成焉。天下之於君身，其相去亦甚懸者，而何至以急於身也？君愛其身，而天下之人亦各自愛其身；君養巳而不先養人，則彼將競起而各求所爲養焉，而天下之事始紛然矣。夫惟不以民視民，而視民猶吾身，於是愛身必先於愛民，而養民尤急於養身，則天下之民始無有不得其所者。夫然後舉天下之民皆委命於其君，而天下可以晏然而無事。然則愛民者，
translation_en:
… the meaning of "nurturing the people while fearing only that it is insufficient" with utmost thoroughness. Moreover, its structure is lofty and its tone archaic, its thought profound and its vigor forceful. This is one who can vigorously reject hollow superficiality and esteem great elegance; it may serve as a model.
Associate Examiner Instructor Huang comments: With an archaic and elegant tone, he expresses incisive and earnest thoughts. This is something beneficial to the principles of governance, and not merely skillful in writing. A fine scholar, a fine scholar!
Examiner Right Admonisher Chen comments: What a discourse! It has command and modulation, bringing out the meaning of how a ruler nurtures the people to achieve peace and order in a nuanced and exhaustive manner. It should be recorded as a model.
Examiner Left Companion Dai comments: Having grasped the crux, its structure is naturally grand and expansive, and its spirit even more flowing and resonant.

The ruler integrates the entire realm into a single body. Therefore, working for the realm is more urgent than working for his own person, and thus the governance of the realm is accomplished. The realm and the ruler's own person are vastly distant from one another; why then should it come to be considered more urgent than his own person? The ruler loves his own person, and the people of the realm likewise each love their own persons. If the ruler nurtures himself without first nurturing others, then they will vie to rise up and each seek the means to nurture themselves, and the affairs of the realm will thereupon fall into turmoil. Only when he does not view the people merely as the people, but views the people as his own body—so that loving his own person necessarily begins with loving the people, and nurturing the people is even more urgent than nurturing his own person—will there begin to be none among the people of the realm who do not find their proper place. Only then will all the people of the realm entrust their lives to their ruler, and the realm can be tranquil and free of trouble. This being so, loving the people…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
固所以自愛而養民者正所以養吾身者歟胡
氏曰養民惟恐不足此世之所以治安也請申
其旨天下大矣天下之民衆矣士農工賈不同
業而皆營貴富賤貧不同勢而皆騁智愚巧拙
不同心而皆慮勇怯利鈍不同力而皆用彼其
所以林林然立總總然聚役役然奔逐於日夜無休
時者何也有是身而欲養之也養是身而恐其
不足也而君人者履無上之位據無外之勢儻
亦欲私其身而猶夫天下之民之心則錦衣玉
===
食以爲奉密房廣廈以爲居管絃金石以爲娛
佳冶窈窕以爲御何不給者顧君之養將於民
乎取之也取之民也多則民之養也必闕闕民
之養以自奉而天下始有不均之患矣甚不均
則貧甚貧則無以聊生而欺紿爲奸爭奪爲梗
之釁作矣君人者孰不以治世安民爲志也而
卒使之至於此何也以爲君至尊也民至卑也
君至貴也民至賤也尊貴其身卑賤其民而不
思其有相爲一體者在也何也蓋有天下而後
punctuated:
固所以自愛，而養民者正所以養吾身者歟！胡氏曰：「養民惟恐不足，此世之所以治安也。」請申其旨。

天下大矣，天下之民衆矣。士、農、工、賈，不同業而皆營；貴、富、賤、貧，不同勢而皆騁；智、愚、巧、拙，不同心而皆慮；勇、怯、利、鈍，不同力而皆用。彼其所以林林然立、總總然聚、役役然奔逐於日夜無休時者，何也？有是身而欲養之也，養是身而恐其不足也。而君人者，履無上之位，據無外之勢，儻亦欲私其身，而猶夫天下之民之心，則錦衣玉食以爲奉，密房廣廈以爲居，管絃金石以爲娛，佳冶窈窕以爲御，何不給者？顧君之養，將於民乎取之也。取之民也多，則民之養也必闕；闕民之養以自奉，而天下始有不均之患矣。甚不均則貧，甚貧則無以聊生，而欺紿爲奸、爭奪爲梗之釁作矣。君人者，孰不以治世安民爲志也？而卒使之至於此，何也？以爲君至尊也，民至卑也；君至貴也，民至賤也。尊貴其身，卑賤其民，而不思其有相爲一體者在也。何也？蓋有天下而後
translation_en:
…is truly the way to love oneself, and nourishing the people is precisely the way to nourish one's own person! Master Hu (Hu Yin 胡寅) said: "In nourishing the people, one only fears that it is insufficient—this is how the world achieves order and peace." Allow me to elaborate on the meaning of this.

The empire is vast, and the people of the empire are multitude. Scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants have different occupations, yet all busily ply their trades; the noble, the rich, the base, and the poor occupy different positions of influence, yet all strive; the wise, the foolish, the skillful, and the clumsy have different minds, yet all lay plans; the brave, the timid, the sharp, and the dull have different strengths, yet all exert them. Why is it that they stand like a dense forest, gather in teeming crowds, and toil and rush about day and night without rest? Because they have these bodies and wish to nourish them, and in nourishing these bodies they fear having less than enough. Now one who rules over others occupies a peerless position and holds all-encompassing power. If he too wished to indulge his own person selfishly, sharing the same mentality as the people of the empire—taking brocade robes and jade-like delicacies for his maintenance, secluded chambers and spacious mansions for his dwelling, pipes, strings, bronze bells, and stone chimes for his amusement, and alluring, graceful beauties for his attendance—what could he possibly lack? Yet the ruler's maintenance must be taken from the people. If what is taken from the people is much, then the people's own nourishment will surely fall short. When the people's nourishment is curtailed to supply oneself, the empire begins to suffer from the ill of inequality. Extreme inequality leads to poverty; extreme poverty leaves the people with nothing by which to sustain their lives, and thus arise the rifts of deceitful villainy and contentious plundering. Among those who rule over others, who does not set his ambition on bringing order to the world and peace to the people? Yet in the end they cause things to come to this pass—why? Because they consider the ruler supremely exalted and the people supremely lowly; the ruler supremely noble and the people supremely base. They exalt and ennoble their own persons while debasing and despising their people, without reflecting on the fact that there is that by which they form a single body with one another. Why is this? Because only when there is the empire…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
可以附吾國有一國而後可以附吾家有一家
而後可以附吾身是家國天下者君身之所寄
也無之是無所寄吾身也然則君與民其庸其
二乎譬之身焉君其元首也家人其肺腑也國
人其胷腹也天下之人其四肢也以其勢則相
須而不可離以其用則相待而不可缺是故君
與民猶一體也養之不可不急也且民又何賴
於君之養也凡養之具不能無待於物而凡物
之用不能無待於所以制之者顧民之愚而智
===
不知所以制也民之卑而力不能爲之制也惟
爲之君者其聰明神聖旣足以調劑物性之所
宜而盡其制而崇高隆重之勢又足以役使羣
動而使之莫敢不聽其制君制其所以養之之
方而後民得守其制以安於其養譬之身焉其
臟腑胷腹四肢具在而所恃以得其養者正以
元首在上目視而耳聽鼻調其噓吸而口善其
吐納也而況乎天下之財生之甚難而靡之甚
易三時疾耕僅免於饑終歲勤織僅免於寒而
punctuated: 可以附吾國，有一國而後可以附吾家，有一家而後可以附吾身。是家國天下者，君身之所寄也；無之，是無所寄吾身也。然則君與民，其庸其二乎？譬之身焉，君其元首也，家人其肺腑也，國人其胷腹也，天下之人其四肢也。以其勢則相須而不可離，以其用則相待而不可缺。是故君與民猶一體也，養之不可不急也。且民又何賴於君之養也？凡養之具，不能無待於物；而凡物之用，不能無待於所以制之者。顧民之愚，而智不知所以制也；民之卑，而力不能爲之制也。惟爲之君者，其聰明神聖旣足以調劑物性之所宜而盡其制，而崇高隆重之勢又足以役使羣動而使之莫敢不聽其制。君制其所以養之之方，而後民得守其制以安於其養。譬之身焉，其臟腑、胷腹、四肢具在，而所恃以得其養者，正以元首在上，目視而耳聽，鼻調其噓吸，而口善其吐納也。而況乎天下之財，生之甚難而靡之甚易，三時疾耕僅免於饑，終歲勤織僅免於寒，而
translation_en:
… can one attach one's state; only after possessing a state can one attach one's family; and only after possessing a family can one attach one's own person. Thus, the family, the state, and the empire are that upon which the ruler's person depends; without them, there is nothing upon which to rest one's person. How then could the ruler and the people possibly be two separate things [?]? To compare it to the body: the ruler is its head, the members of the family are its lungs and viscera, the people of the capital are its chest and abdomen, and the people of the empire are its four limbs. In their positional relationship, they need one another and cannot be separated; in their function, they rely on one another and none can be lacking. Therefore, the ruler and the people are like a single body, and nourishing them cannot but be an urgent priority.

Moreover, why do the people depend upon the ruler for their nourishment? All the means of nourishment must rely on material things, and all uses of material things must rely on that which regulates them. Yet because the people are simple, their wisdom does not know how to regulate them; because the people are lowly, their strength is unable to establish regulations for them. Only the one who acts as their ruler possesses the intelligence and sagely wisdom sufficient to harmonize what is suitable in the nature of things and bring their regulation to perfection, as well as the exalted and weighty authority sufficient to command all active beings so that none dare disobey his regulations. Only after the ruler establishes the methods by which they are nourished can the people abide by his regulations and rest secure in their nourishment. To compare it to the body: its internal organs, chest and abdomen, and four limbs are all present, yet what they rely upon to obtain their nourishment is precisely that the head is above, with the eyes seeing and the ears hearing, the nose regulating its exhalations and inhalations, and the mouth skillfully managing what it takes in and lets out.

How much more is this the case when the wealth of the empire is very difficult to produce and very easy to squander! Toiling at the plow through the three agricultural seasons barely spares one from hunger, and diligently weaving throughout the entire year barely spares one from cold, while…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
水旱癘札冦賊之虞又常出於不意儲稍不豫
卽索然匱矣譬之身焉一日不哺則腹爲之枵
而或寒暑燥濕之變一有不調卽疾痛生焉然
則養民又如之何其有足時也君人者知民之
不可一日失養而養之之本在農也是以重其
事不奪其時寛其役不竭其力薄其歛不匱其
有田里之旣授而郵表坊庸之具亦無不修播
種之旣戒而耘耔刈獲之時亦無不省倉廪之
旣登而祈穀祈年之祀亦無不豫九年之旣積
===
而不足非國之戒亦不敢忘生齒之旣繁而冗
食冗費之端亦不敢啓而又老疾有饑貧乏有
賑逐末有罰淫巧有刑人侵則蠲其賦租大災
則䝱其厲禁蓋其君臣日夜之所講求政事大
小之所施措無一非爲養民之計恐恐然常懼
有一人之不得保其性命而一日之不得安其
生理者夫然後爲之民者得以不遷於異物而
不起夫奸萌安其心於本業而畢其力於南畝
由是穀乃豐登年乃順成而積貯日富矣由是
punctuated: 水旱、癘札、冦賊之虞，又常出於不意，儲稍不豫，卽索然匱矣。譬之身焉，一日不哺，則腹爲之枵；而或寒暑燥濕之變，一有不調，卽疾痛生焉。然則養民又如之何其有足時也？君人者，知民之不可一日失養，而養之之本在農也，是以重其事，不奪其時；寛其役，不竭其力；薄其歛，不匱其有。田里之旣授，而郵表坊庸之具亦無不修；播種之旣戒，而耘耔刈獲之時亦無不省；倉廪之旣登，而祈穀祈年之祀亦無不豫；九年之旣積，而不足非國之戒亦不敢忘；生齒之旣繁，而冗食冗費之端亦不敢啓。而又老疾有饑，貧乏有賑，逐末有罰，淫巧有刑，人侵則蠲其賦租，大災則䝱其厲禁。蓋其君臣日夜之所講求，政事大小之所施措，無一非爲養民之計，恐恐然常懼有一人之不得保其性命，而一日之不得安其生理者。夫然後爲之民者，得以不遷於異物，而不起夫奸萌，安其心於本業，而畢其力於南畝。由是穀乃豐登，年乃順成，而積貯日富矣；由是
translation_en: … the perils of flood and drought, pestilence and premature death, and bandits and rebels also constantly arise unexpectedly; if reserves are not prepared even slightly in advance, everything is utterly exhausted. Compare this to the human body: if for a single day it is not fed, the belly goes empty; and should there be changes of cold, heat, dryness, or dampness, the slightest imbalance immediately gives rise to sickness and pain. This being so, how then could there ever be a time when the nourishment of the people is sufficient of itself? Those who rule over others know that the people cannot go a single day without nourishment, and that the foundation of nourishing them lies in agriculture. Therefore, they treat their tasks as weighty and do not rob them of their seasonal hours; they relax their corvée labor and do not exhaust their strength; they make their exactions light and do not deplete what they possess. Once fields and homesteads have been allotted, the facilities of field-huts, boundary markers, dikes, and ditches are without exception kept in repair; once sowing and planting have been enjoined, the seasons of weeding, banking up roots, and harvesting are without exception inspected; once the granaries have been filled, the sacrifices praying for grain and for a good year are without exception prepared in advance; once nine years' reserves have been accumulated, the warning that a state without sufficient stores is not truly a state is still not dared to be forgotten; once the population has grown numerous, avenues of superfluous eaters and superfluous expenditures are still not dared to be opened. Furthermore, the aged and infirm receive gifts of grain [? 饑 for 餼], the poor and destitute receive relief, those who pursue secondary occupations are fined, those who practice extravagant contrivances are punished; when famine strikes [? 人侵 for 大祲], their taxes and rents are remitted, and when great calamities occur, rigorous prohibitions are relaxed [? 䝱 for 弛]. Indeed, all that the ruler and his ministers deliberate upon day and night, and all that is enacted in government affairs great and small, is without exception a plan for nourishing the people—anxiously and constantly fearing lest even a single person fail to preserve his life, or fail for a single day to rest secure in his livelihood. Only then can those who are the people avoid being enticed away by novel things and refrain from giving rise to the sprouts of wickedness, setting their hearts at ease in their fundamental occupation and devoting all their strength to the southern acres. From this, the grain is abundantly harvested, the year comes to seasonable fruition, and stored reserves grow richer by the day; from this…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
老者以養幼者以長而婦子日寧矣由是財勝
其賦力勝其役而國用日充矣由是廉恥日長
禮義日生而教化可行矣由是協氣充塞瑞應
駢臻而禮樂可興矣由是端拱穆清揖讓羣后
而爲君者可以恭已無爲矣譬之身焉氣充於
臓腑而神爽發於面目脉暢於四肢而華澤溢
於顔表故曰民富而國富民安而君安也蓋自
古治安之道必考信於詩書而詩書所稱繼世
之盛莫如周成王然無逸一篇惟諄切於稼穡
之艱難七月之咏其於耕夫工女之事至纖悉
矣而制度文章之事不與焉蓋誠以爲養民者
致治之本而制度文章皆所以維持其爲養之
具也故成王之世刑措不用者數十年逮漢文
景勸農之詔數下而三老力田之勞賜相望於
歲時至於賜民田租之半或遂除焉於是國以
殷富獄以空虚幾與成王比隆蓋務養民之明
效有如此者自時厥後不思所以養之而惟務
所以取之取之而不能繼於是一切苟且之術
punctuated: 老者以養，幼者以長，而婦子日寧矣；由是財勝其賦，力勝其役，而國用日充矣；由是廉恥日長，禮義日生，而教化可行矣；由是協氣充塞，瑞應駢臻，而禮樂可興矣；由是端拱穆清，揖讓羣后，而爲君者可以恭已無爲矣。譬之身焉，氣充於臓腑，而神爽發於面目，脉暢於四肢，而華澤溢於顔表。故曰：民富而國富，民安而君安也。蓋自古治安之道，必考信於《詩》、《書》，而《詩》、《書》所稱繼世之盛，莫如周成王。然《無逸》一篇，惟諄切於稼穡之艱難；《七月》之咏，其於耕夫工女之事，至纖悉矣，而制度文章之事不與焉。蓋誠以爲養民者，致治之本，而制度文章，皆所以維持其爲養之具也。故成王之世，刑措不用者數十年。逮漢文、景，勸農之詔數下，而三老、力田之勞賜，相望於歲時，至於賜民田租之半，或遂除焉。於是國以殷富，獄以空虚，幾與成王比隆。蓋務養民之明效，有如此者。自時厥後，不思所以養之，而惟務所以取之；取之而不能繼，於是一切苟且之術，
translation_en:
…the elderly are thereby nourished, the young are thereby raised, and wives and children grow more peaceful by the day; from this, wealth exceeds the taxes levied, strength exceeds the labor services required, and state finances grow fuller by the day; from this, a sense of integrity and shame grows daily, propriety and righteousness arise daily, and moral transformation can be carried out; from this, harmonious vital energy fills the realm, auspicious omens arrive side by side, and rites and music can be made to flourish; from this, sitting upright with folded hands in solemn tranquility and exchanging courtesies with the assembled lords, the ruler can simply remain reverent in himself and rule through non-action. Compare it to the human body: when vital energy fills the internal organs, spirited vigor radiates from the face and eyes; when the pulse flows freely through the four limbs, a lustrous glow overflows upon the countenance. Therefore it is said: when the people are rich, the state is rich; when the people are secure, the ruler is secure.

Indeed, since antiquity, the way of order and peace has always been verified in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu), and among the flourishing reigns of succeeding generations praised in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents, none surpassed that of King Cheng of Zhou. Yet the chapter "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi) speaks earnestly only of the hardships of sowing and reaping, while the ode "Seventh Month" (Qiyue) is detailed to the utmost regarding the labors of plowmen and weaving women, without touching upon matters of institutional systems and cultural adornment. This is truly because nourishing the people was regarded as the root of achieving good governance, whereas institutional systems and cultural adornment were all merely instruments for maintaining that nourishment. Thus, in the reign of King Cheng, punishments were set aside and unused for several decades. Coming down to Emperors Wen and Jing of the Han, edicts encouraging agriculture were repeatedly issued, and rewards and comforting gifts for the Thrice Venerable (sanlao) and the Diligent Cultivators (litian) followed one after another throughout the seasons and years, even going so far as to grant the people a remission of half their land tax, or at times abolishing it altogether. Thereupon, the state became prosperous and rich, and the prisons became empty, nearly matching the splendor of King Cheng. Such was the clear efficacy of devoting effort to nourishing the people. From that time onward, rulers did not ponder how to nourish them, but devoted themselves solely to how to extract from them; when they extracted from them and could not sustain it, every sort of expedient and makeshift technique…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
畢用而民生日蹙世事日非矣譬猶剔決體膚
以滋口吻其存能幾何也嗚呼天下之物必有
所生而後可用必有所積而後可資其積之也
厚則資之也愈久不先其所生積而資與用焉
之是急以此求治毋亦倒行而逆計也哉然則
人君欲養其民當何如主之以成王之無逸而
持之以文景之節儉其可也此養民之本也
表
擬宋命蔡襄寫尚書無逸篇于邇英延義
閣屏羣臣賀表景祐二年
===
陳所藴
同考試官教諭林　批〔闡無逸意莊雅駢麗〕
同考試官教諭汪　批〔體格渾融詞華駢麗　且忠懇之心藹然四六之名家也〕
同考試官教諭鄧　批〔詞章富麗音律鏗鏘　是善發無逸之旨者非徒四六之工而已〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔駢麗有則寫出無逸　尚書無逸闡揚盡矣表學之工者錄之〕
punctuated:
畢用，而民生日蹙，世事日非矣。譬猶剔決體膚以滋口吻，其存能幾何也！嗚呼！天下之物，必有所生而後可用，必有所積而後可資；其積之也厚，則資之也愈久。不先其所生積，而資與用焉之是急，以此求治，毋亦倒行而逆計也哉！然則人君欲養其民，當何如？主之以成王之《無逸》，而持之以文、景之節儉，其可也。此養民之本也。

表
擬宋命蔡襄寫《尚書》《無逸》篇于邇英、延義閣屏羣臣賀表（景祐二年）
陳所藴
同考試官教諭林　批〔闡《無逸》意，莊雅駢麗。〕
同考試官教諭汪　批〔體格渾融，詞華駢麗，且忠懇之心藹然，四六之名家也。〕
同考試官教諭鄧　批〔詞章富麗，音律鏗鏘，是善發《無逸》之旨者，非徒四六之工而已。〕
同考試官教諭王　批〔駢麗有則，寫出《無逸》。《尚書》《無逸》闡揚盡矣，表學之工者，錄之。〕
translation_en:
… were all employed, so that the people's livelihood grew daily more straitened and the affairs of the world daily more awry. It is like carving away one's own flesh and skin to nourish the mouth—how long can one survive! Alas! The things of the world must first be produced before they can be used, and must first be accumulated before they can be drawn upon; the more richly they are accumulated, the longer they can be drawn upon. Not to put production and accumulation first, while urgently pressing to draw upon and use them—to seek good governance in this way, is that not acting perversely and calculating backward? How, then, ought a ruler who wishes to nourish his people proceed? Let him take King Cheng's "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi) as his guiding principle, and uphold it with the frugality of Emperors Wen and Jing, and that will suffice. This is the foundation of nourishing the people.

Memorial
Imitating a congratulatory memorial from the assembled officials upon the Song dynasty's commanding Cai Xiang 蔡襄 to transcribe the "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi 無逸) chapter of the Book of Documents (Shangshu 尚書) onto the screens of the Erying and Yanyi Pavilions (Second year of the Jingyou reign, 1035).

By Chen Suoyun 陳所藴.

Associate Examiner and Instructor Lin comments: "It expounds the meaning of 'Against Luxurious Ease' in a dignified, refined, and richly parallel style."
Associate Examiner and Instructor Wang comments: "Its structure is harmoniously integrated, its diction ornately parallel, and a loyal, earnest heart shines warmly through—truly a master of four-six parallel prose."
Associate Examiner and Instructor Deng comments: "Its literary expression is sumptuous and its cadence resonant. This is one who excels at bringing out the purport of 'Against Luxurious Ease,' not merely skilled in four-six parallel prose."
Associate Examiner and Instructor Wang comments: "Parallel and ornate yet observing proper norms, it vividly portrays 'Against Luxurious Ease.' [Note: Actually, two lines from the next page's column seem swapped in woodblock/transcription order here: 'The Against Luxurious Ease chapter of the Book of Documents is fully elucidated; a masterwork of memorial composition—let it be recorded.' …]"

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
情狀宛然如見善體周公忠愛之心者
矣
考試官右贊善陳　批〔詞典則而旨微婉可以式〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔典雅可式〕
景祐二年正月癸丑日臣某等恭睹
上命蔡襄寫尚書無逸篇于邇英延義閣屛臣
等誠懽誠忭稽首頓首稱
賀者伏惟
王業勤民爰示顯哉之訓
===
聖心勵政允資顧諟之明治不可以忘危道莫
尚於師古簡編存鑒
黼扆生輝竊惟哲后嗣興必儆盈成之象老
臣謀國能多微漸之防故總章衢室之風
于今尚㮄戶楹銘鐸之屬從古有銘昔成
王踐位于冲齡方向日中之運周公矢忠
以匡辟獨先天下之憂思聖學之始終克
由抑畏而王業之根本起自艱難首陳無
逸之章歷述先朝之蹟凡稼穡田功之疾
punctuated:
情狀宛然如見，善體周公忠愛之心者矣。
考試官右贊善陳　批〔詞典則而旨微婉，可以式。〕
考試官左中允戴　批〔典雅可式。〕
景祐二年正月癸丑日，臣某等恭睹上命蔡襄寫《尚書》《無逸》篇于邇英、延義閣屛，臣等誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首，稱賀者。伏惟王業勤民，爰示顯哉之訓；聖心勵政，允資顧諟之明。治不可以忘危，道莫尚於師古。簡編存鑒，黼扆生輝。竊惟哲后嗣興，必儆盈成之象；老臣謀國，能多微漸之防。故總章、衢室之風，于今尚㮄；戶楹、銘鐸之屬，從古有銘。昔成王踐位于冲齡，方向日中之運；周公矢忠以匡辟，獨先天下之憂。思聖學之始終，克由抑畏；而王業之根本，起自艱難。首陳《無逸》之章，歷述先朝之蹟。凡稼穡田功之疾…
translation_en:
…the circumstances and demeanor as vividly as if seen before one's eyes—truly one who has well grasped the loyal and affectionate heart of the Duke of Zhou.

Examiner, Right Admonisher Chen, comments: "The diction is classical and regular, and the purport is subtle and tactful; it may serve as a model."
Examiner, Left Companion Dai, comments: "Classically elegant; it may serve as a model."

On the guichou day of the first month of the second year of the Jingyou reign [1035], Your Servants So-and-So and others respectfully witnessed His Majesty command Cai Xiang 蔡襄 to transcribe the "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi 無逸) chapter of the Book of Documents (Shangshu 尚書) upon the screens of the Yanying and Yanyi Pavilions. Filled with genuine joy and elation, Your Servants bow our heads to the ground and offer our congratulations:

We humbly reflect that the royal enterprise lies in diligence toward the people, and thus sets forth these resplendent instructions; the sagely mind exerts itself in governance, and truly relies upon the clear insight of keeping the Mandate ever in view. In a time of order one must never forget danger, and in the Way of rule nothing surpasses taking antiquity as one's teacher. The bamboo slips preserve a mirror for reflection, and the imperial screen shines with added radiance.

We venture to reflect that when a wise sovereign succeeds to the throne and rises to rule, he must ever be on guard against the signs of fullness and completion; and when a veteran minister takes counsel for the state, he is able to multiply precautions against subtle and gradual decline. Thus the customs of the Hall of Light (Zongzhang) and the Audience Chamber (Qushi) are still posted on placards to this day [?], and things such as doors, pillars, inscribed vessels, and warning bells have borne admonition-inscriptions since antiquity.

Of old, when King Cheng ascended the throne in his tender years, facing the flourishing fortune of the sun at its zenith, the Duke of Zhou pledged his loyalty to assist his sovereign and was alone in worrying before the rest of the world worried. Reflecting that the beginning and end of sagely learning can only be achieved through self-restraint and reverent awe, and that the foundation of the royal enterprise arises out of hardship and toil, he first set forth the chapter "Against Luxurious Ease," recounting in turn the deeds of former reigns. All the sufferings of sowing, reaping, and work in the fields…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
苦旣極形容若壽年國祚之短長尤加反
覆迪哲稱四人之治恒寓夫箴規傳心法
三后之賢無嫌于忌諱咏嘆再三而語彌
切吏端有七而慮愈深顧載籍雖遺號右
文者弗研于往牒淵源斯遠誦微言者竟
襲于空談非籍
熙朝曷昭
彝典茲蓋伏遇
===
資由神授
德與性生暑御
經帷仰文心之翼翼禮隆
慈幄敦舜孝之夔夔郤異物以念農遇天災而
策士西疇刈麥憫小民之無依
秘館說書受直言之如渴頃因
萬幾之暇用規二閣之成
偉制聿新
嘉名載錫式爲鑒往匪曰榮觀謂周公事君
punctuated: 苦，旣極形容；若壽年國祚之短長，尤加反覆。迪哲稱四人之治，恒寓夫箴規；傳心法三后之賢，無嫌于忌諱。咏嘆再三而語彌切，吏端有七而慮愈深。顧載籍雖遺，號右文者弗研于往牒；淵源斯遠，誦微言者竟襲于空談。非籍熙朝，曷昭彝典？茲蓋伏遇資由神授，德與性生。暑御經帷，仰文心之翼翼；禮隆慈幄，敦舜孝之夔夔。郤異物以念農，遇天災而策士。西疇刈麥，憫小民之無依；秘館說書，受直言之如渴。頃因萬幾之暇，用規二閣之成。偉制聿新，嘉名載錫；式爲鑒往，匪曰榮觀。謂周公事君，
translation_en:
… hardships of farming and agricultural labor were described to the utmost; as for the length or brevity of lifespans and reigns, he reiterated this repeatedly. In praising the rule of the four kings who walked in wisdom, he constantly embedded admonitions; in transmitting the mind-method and modeling on the worthiness of the three rulers, he did not shy away from taboos. Sighing in exclamation again and again, his words grew ever more earnest; through seven changes of topic [reading 更端 for 吏端?], his concerns ran ever deeper. Yet although the written records survive, those who claim to champion letters do not study the past documents; as the source has grown distant, those who recite the subtle words ultimately fall into empty talk. Were it not for reliance on our Glorious Dynasty, how could this constant canon be made bright?

This is indeed because we humbly encounter Your Majesty, whose endowments are divinely bestowed, and whose virtue is born with Your nature. In the summer heat You attend the Classics Mat, where we look up to the reverent care of King Wen's heart; with elevated rites at the Maternal Curtain, You cultivate the respectful awe of Shun's filial piety. You reject exotic curiosities out of concern for farming, and upon encountering natural disasters You examine scholars with policy questions. When wheat is reaped in the western fields, You pity the common people for having naught to rely on; when books are expounded in the Imperial Library, You receive forthright words as if thirsty. Recently, during leisure from Your myriad affairs of state, You planned the completion of the two pavilions. The grand structure is newly built, and auspicious names have been bestowed upon them; they serve as a mirror of the past, not merely as a splendid sight. You deemed that the Duke of Zhou's service to his sovereign…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
萬世之所當法而無逸進誡一言可以興
邦但輿義具夫精微允宜
燕閒之頻接全經託諸簡冊限於講讀之有
時乃取孫奭之圖更屬蔡襄之筆探奇珍
於孔壁大揮
便殿之素屛昉遺軌于殷盤特借尚方之彤
管文華陳其上下豈謂無徵義備錄夫後
先是求有益書成
左右編
===
至函石室之藏翰灑淸華晃
寶構璘䃲之宇治源亂本無勞竹素之旁搜
主德民情時覩羮墻之有在昔
皇祖興崇文于內院
懿範猶傳暨
眞考萃羣書于禁林芳䂓未泯矧逢
今日更衍前庥
法從逶臨宛若呈圖書於河洛簪裾儼集恍
然悟心畫於丹靑非備一時文獻之詳侈
punctuated: 萬世之所當法，而《無逸》進誡，一言可以興邦；但輿義具夫精微，允宜燕閒之頻接，全經託諸簡冊，限於講讀之有時。乃取孫奭之圖，更屬蔡襄之筆；探奇珍於孔壁，大揮便殿之素屛；昉遺軌于殷盤，特借尚方之彤管。文華陳其上下，豈謂無徵；義備錄夫後先，是求有益。書成左右，編至函石室之藏；翰灑淸華，晃寶構璘䃲之宇。治源亂本，無勞竹素之旁搜；主德民情，時覩羮墻之有在。昔皇祖興崇文于內院，懿範猶傳；暨眞考萃羣書于禁林，芳䂓未泯。矧逢今日，更衍前庥。法從逶臨，宛若呈圖書於河洛；簪裾儼集，恍然悟心畫於丹靑。非備一時文獻之詳，侈
translation_en: … is what ought to be taken as a model for ten thousand generations, and the admonitions presented in "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi) are such that a single phrase can bring prosperity to a state. However, while its profound meanings possess the utmost subtlety—making it truly fitting for frequent engagement during moments of leisure—the complete Classic is entrusted to bamboo slips and books, which limits its exposition and reading to set times. Thereupon, Your Majesty took the diagrams of Sun Shi 孫奭 and further entrusted them to the brush of Cai Xiang 蔡襄; seeking out rare treasures from the wall of Confucius's house, You had them grandly inscribed across the plain screens of the side palace halls; imitating the surviving model of the basins of Yin, You specially borrowed the red-lacquered brushes of the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories. With literary brilliance setting forth what is above and below, how could it be said to lack verification? With righteous principles fully recorded from beginning to end, this indeed seeks what is beneficial. The calligraphy is completed to the left and right, and the compilations reach to the holdings encased in the stone chambers; the brush-strokes are sprinkled in pure splendor, illuminating the variegated eaves of the precious structures. For the springs of good governance and the roots of disorder, there is no need to toil in searching far and wide through bamboo slips and silk scrolls; the sovereign's virtue and the people's conditions are constantly seen, as though present in one's soup and on one's walls. In the past, the Imperial Ancestor established the Hall for Venerating Literature (Chongwen) in the inner court, and his admirable model is still handed down; and when the True Ancestor gathered the multitude of books in the forbidden grove, his fragrant regulations have not perished. How much more so now that we meet with the present day, which further extends the blessings of the past! When the imperialcortège winds its way to attend, it is just as if the Diagram and Writing were being presented from the Yellow and Luo Rivers; when officials in hairpins and robes solemnly assemble, they suddenly awaken to the paintings of the mind in vermilion and blue. This is not merely to provide a detailed array of the documents and worthies of a single age, indulging in…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
博綜而鶩粉飾寔究二代典刑之故鏡孅
惡而照興衰入以省出以觀炳炳皆景行
哲王之地感而思思而懼時時為游心邃
古之資彼石渠天祿之設徒聞疑闕未闢
緊長夜太液之箴雖善蒙牖猶扃未若抒
秘典于緗緗戶綴丹書之藻列徽猷于鉛
槧案披紫府之文儻
陟降不違非比韋弦之小助方儀形如見詎
云明鑑之有功信
===
英君誼辟之宏摹而
聖子神孫之世寶也〔臣〕等躬逢
盛事秖鷩麗翰之昭回忝列清班仰侍
黈旒之瞻對敢不竭傃惠教誨之大義少罄
揄揚服危明戒盛之訏謨上酬
顧問伏願
典學有獲
主善惟師知帝王之道在憂勤創守仰稽乎
千聖念閭閻之狀多隱伏怠荒時勑于
punctuated: 博綜而鶩粉飾，寔究二代典刑之故，鏡孅惡而照興衰。入以省，出以觀，炳炳皆景行哲王之地；感而思，思而懼，時時為游心邃古之資。彼石渠、天祿之設，徒聞疑闕未闢，緊長夜、太液之箴，雖善蒙牖猶扃；未若抒秘典于緗緗，戶綴丹書之藻，列徽猷于鉛槧，案披紫府之文。儻陟降不違，非比韋弦之小助；方儀形如見，詎云明鑑之有功？信英君誼辟之宏摹，而聖子神孫之世寶也。〔臣〕等躬逢盛事，秖鷩麗翰之昭回；忝列清班，仰侍黈旒之瞻對。敢不竭傃惠教誨之大義，少罄揄揚；服危明戒盛之訏謨，上酬顧問。伏願典學有獲，主善惟師。知帝王之道在憂勤，創守仰稽乎千聖；念閭閻之狀多隱伏，怠荒時勑于
translation_en:
… boasting of wide-ranging synthesis or chasing after superficial embellishment, it truly investigates the causes behind the institutions and models of the two dynasties, mirroring the slightest evils and illuminating rise and fall. Entering to examine them, going out to observe them, brightly everywhere is a place to emulate the wise kings of old; moved to reflect, and reflecting with trepidation, at every moment they serve as an aid for letting the mind roam in remote antiquity. Those establishments of the Stone Canal (Shiqu) and Heavenly Emolument (Tianlu) pavilions merely heard of doubts and lacunae without resolving them, while the admonitions of the Long Night (Changye) and the Taiye Pool, though fine, left the darkened window still bolted. None of that compares to unfolding secret canons in pale yellow silk wraps, where every door is adorned with the artistry of the Cinnabar Book, and arraying glorious counsels on lead and wooden tablets, where every desk opens the writings of the Purple Palace. Should Your Majesty abide by them in ascending and descending without fail, this is no mere minor aid like the soft leather and taut bowstring; when their exemplary forms appear right before Your eyes, how could one say that only a bright mirror has merit? Truly this is a grand design for heroic sovereigns and righteous rulers, and a hereditary treasure for sacred sons and divine grandsons!

Your servants have personally encountered this magnificent event, respectfully admiring the resplendent revolution of these beautiful writings; unworthily ranked in the pure courtly procession, we look up in attendance before the imperial crown with its yellow-silk ear-plugs. How dare we not exhaust the great principle of loving kindness and instruction to offer a small measure of praise, and take to heart the grand counsels of maintaining clarity in peril and guarding against fullness at the height of prosperity in order to answer Your Majesty's inquiries above? We humbly pray that Your Majesty may gain from constant study and take goodness alone as Your teacher; that You may know that the Way of emperors and kings lies in anxious diligence, looking up to examine how the thousand sages founded and preserved their realms; and that You may bear in mind how the conditions of the common people in their lanes and alleys are largely hidden from view, constantly warning against indolence and neglect within…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
九重旰食不遑省終日于盤之失恫瘝在念
以庶邦惟正之供則
君德罔愆不假彌文之迹爾
天命自度信嫓有道之隆臣無任瞻
天仰
聖忻躍屛營之至謹奉
表稱
賀以
聞
===
第叁場
策五道
第一問
同考試官教諭王　批我
史繼辰
聖上以冲齡得心學之純
奎章
宸翰嫓休哉
皇祖肴信不常之彝典萬世之希遘也是作不獨闡發懿美詳盡且
punctuated:
九重。旰食不遑，省終日于盤之失；恫瘝在念，以庶邦惟正之供。則君德罔愆，不假彌文之迹；爾天命自度，信嫓有道之隆。臣無任瞻天仰聖，忻躍屛營之至，謹奉表稱賀以聞。

第叁場
策五道
第一問
史繼辰
同考試官教諭王批：我聖上以冲齡得心學之純，奎章宸翰，嫓休哉皇祖肴，信不常之彝典、萬世之希遘也。是作不獨闡發懿美詳盡，且
translation_en:
… within the Ninefold Palace. Eating late without leisure, examine the lapses of spending the whole day in pleasure; keeping the sufferings of the people in mind, accept only the regular tribute from the myriad states. Then the sovereign's virtue will be without fault, having no need for the traces of superficial ornament; and in measuring Yourself by Heaven's Mandate [?], You will truly rival the flourishing era of a ruler who possesses the Way. Your servant, overwhelmed to the utmost with gazing upon Heaven and looking up to the Sage in joyful excitement and reverent trepidation, respectfully presents this memorial of congratulation for Your Majesty's hearing.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions
First Question
Shi Jichen 史繼辰
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Wang 王: Our Sacred Sovereign, at a young age, has attained the purity of the Learning of the Mind. His imperial compositions and brushwork rival in excellence those of our August Ancestor [?]; truly this is an extraordinary canonical model and a rare encounter in ten thousand generations. This essay not only elaborates upon these admirable splendors in full detail, but also…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
忠悃之念懇懇可録爲
聖脩之助
同考試官教諭伍　批　〔古帝王務學爲急哉〕
皇上宸翰煥發書以載道誠上紹隆古而同符
太祖者此作不惟敷揚盛美而復以法
祖規之忠愛之意溢於言表録之
同考試官教諭李　批　〔我〕
皇上精一天啓問學日新眞同符
太祖而陋漢唐宋於不足言者子敷揚懿煥頌繼以規豈懷忠而思
獻者乎
===
考試官右贊善陳　批　〔我〕
皇上英年嗜學眞出天縱子闡揚能識其大而終篇惓惓以法
祖爲
今日望具見忠悃録之不特以文也
考試官左中允戴　批　〔此作敷揚我〕
皇上聖學甚悉而末復以法
祖爲
聖脩助忠愛溢乎辭矣宜録以
punctuated:
忠悃之念懇懇，可録爲聖脩之助。

同考試官教諭伍　批：〔古帝王務學爲急哉，〕皇上宸翰煥發，書以載道，誠上紹隆古而同符太祖者。此作不惟敷揚盛美，而復以法祖規之，忠愛之意溢於言表，録之。

同考試官教諭李　批：〔我〕皇上精一天啓，問學日新，眞同符太祖，而陋漢、唐、宋於不足言者。子敷揚懿煥，頌繼以規，豈懷忠而思獻者乎？

考試官右贊善陳　批：〔我〕皇上英年嗜學，眞出天縱。子闡揚能識其大，而終篇惓惓以法祖爲今日望，具見忠悃。録之，不特以文也。

考試官左中允戴　批：〔此作敷揚我〕皇上聖學甚悉，而末復以法祖爲聖脩助，忠愛溢乎辭矣，宜録以
translation_en:
…its feelings of loyal sincerity are earnest and heartfelt; it is worthy of being recorded as an aid to His Majesty's sage self-cultivation.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Wu: [Ancient emperors and kings treated devotion to learning as an urgent priority! (or: For ancient emperors and kings, devotion to learning was urgent; As for our...)] His Majesty's imperial calligraphy shines forth brilliantly, using writing to convey the Way; truly he continues the heritage of high antiquity above and matches the Grand Progenitor (Taizu). This essay not only sets forth and extols this flourishing excellence, but also offers admonition by urging the emulation of the Imperial Ancestor. A spirit of loyalty and affection overflows beyond the words. Record it.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Li: [Our] Emperor, his pure and unified mind opened by Heaven, renews his inquiry and learning day by day; truly he matches the Grand Progenitor and makes Han, Tang, and Song seem paltry and not worth mentioning. The candidate sets forth and extols this admirable brilliance, following praise with admonition—is he not one who cherishes loyalty and wishes to present it to the throne?

Comment by Examiner and Right Admonisher Chen: [Our] Emperor in his youthful prime delights in learning, a gift that truly comes from Heaven. In expounding and extolling this, the candidate is able to recognize what is of great importance, and at the end of the piece he earnestly takes emulating the Imperial Ancestor as his hope for today, which fully reveals his loyal sincerity. We record it, and not merely for its literary style.

Comment by Examiner and Left Companion Dai: [This essay sets forth and extols our] Emperor's sage learning in great detail, and at the end again offers the emulation of the Imperial Ancestor as an aid to His Majesty's sage self-cultivation. Loyalty and affection overflow in its phrasing; it ought to be recorded in order to…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
獻
聖人有主敬之實心達顯微而無間有體
物之實學貫道藝而具存夫聖人之心運
量天地綜緯萬機有一息之停乎然怡情
於游息亦所以培昭曠之原聖人之學綸
絡古今統承千聖豈一物之察乎然習勤
於藻翰亦所以為燕間之助故大廷非顯
也深宮非隱也惟於幽獨之中而不忘古
訓之式則知微之顯而其心為益純道固
===
成而上也藝非成而下也惟於玩物之會
而不忘儆戒之思則貫道於藝而其功為
益密知此則一張一弛莫非聖修之存而
一點一畫亦皆養德之具矣請因明問而
敬陳之蓋聞上古帝軒刻輿几以謹違大
禹勒筍簴以招諫成湯著日新之戒武王
服敬勝之規其文傳其器朽矣然因其遺
文想其至意則單言隻詞之存固有宛若
羹墻之見者是以後世慕古之君又以銘
punctuated:
獻。
聖人有主敬之實心，達顯微而無間；有體物之實學，貫道藝而具存。夫聖人之心，運量天地，綜緯萬機，有一息之停乎？然怡情於游息，亦所以培昭曠之原。聖人之學，綸絡古今，統承千聖，豈一物之察乎？然習勤於藻翰，亦所以為燕間之助。故大廷非顯也，深宮非隱也，惟於幽獨之中而不忘古訓之式，則知微之顯，而其心為益純；道固成而上也，藝非成而下也，惟於玩物之會而不忘儆戒之思，則貫道於藝，而其功為益密。知此，則一張一弛莫非聖修之存，而一點一畫亦皆養德之具矣。請因明問而敬陳之。蓋聞上古帝軒刻輿几以謹違，大禹勒筍簴以招諫，成湯著日新之戒，武王服敬勝之規，其文傳，其器朽矣。然因其遺文，想其至意，則單言隻詞之存，固有宛若羹墻之見者。是以後世慕古之君，又以銘
translation_en:
…present it to the throne.]

The sage possesses a substantive mind anchored in reverence, reaching through both the manifest and the subtle without interruption; he possesses a substantive learning that embodies things, penetrating both the Way and the arts so that both are preserved together. Now, the mind of the sage encompasses heaven and earth and weaves together the myriad affairs of state—does it ever pause for a single breath? Yet delighting the spirit in recreation and rest is also a means to nourish the source of bright and broad understanding. The learning of the sage threads together antiquity and the present and continues the succession of a thousand sages—how could it be merely the investigation of a single thing? Yet practicing diligence with brush and literary composition is also a means to serve as an aid during moments of leisure. Therefore, the great court is not alone what is manifest, and the deep palace is not alone what is hidden; only when, in solitude and seclusion, one does not forget the model of ancient precepts does one know the manifestness of the subtle, and one's mind becomes ever more pure. What takes form above is indeed the Way, yet the arts are not merely what takes form below; only when, at the moment of engaging with external things, one does not forget thoughts of caution and admonition does one thread the Way through the arts, and one's effort becomes ever more thorough. Understanding this, every tension and every relaxation is nothing less than the preservation of sagely self-cultivation, and every dot and every stroke is likewise an instrument for nourishing virtue. Allow me to respectfully set this forth in response to Your enlightened inquiry.

I have heard that in high antiquity the Yellow Emperor engraved his carriage and stool to guard against transgression, Great Yu inscribed his bell-stands to invite remonstrance, Tang the Successful set forth his admonition on daily renewal, and King Wu took to heart the precept of reverence overcoming negligence. Their words have been transmitted, though their vessels have decayed. Yet if through their surviving words one contemplates their ultimate intent, then the preservation of a single phrase or isolated expression truly makes it seem as though one were seeing them before one's eyes in soup or on a wall. For this reason, rulers of later ages who admired antiquity furthermore felt that inscribing…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
孟未足以廣心燕溺必至於廢學於是或
息肩於藝苑或稅駕於墨池習之雖曰奪
時爲之愈於棄日程子曰寫字時甚敬只
此是學柳氏曰運筆在心心正則筆正孰
謂藝文之末非心學之寓也哉自漢以降
宸翰奎章代有合作或用以當顰咲或寓
以代瞽矇於是紙落人間重於彝鼎矣試
舉執事所及者漢光武賜郡國手書一札
十行皆細書成文而天下風其節儉唐文
===
皇賜衛公手墨大字數幅皆談兵問疾而
將帥效於鼓鞞戴至德爲西臺侍郎而唐
高宗手書飛白賜之曰汎洪源侯舟楫蓋
倚毗之殷也李至勤御書千文而宋眞宗
畋書孝經賜之曰有資教化莫若孝經蓋
敦本之致也之數君者意非不勤矣然或
玩之以溺志終非主敬之實心書非不工
矣然或侈之以競長終非體物之實學本
之則無蓋亦藝焉耳已非眞足以補身心
punctuated: 孟未足以廣心，燕溺必至於廢學。於是或息肩於藝苑，或稅駕於墨池，習之雖曰奪時，爲之愈於棄日。程子曰：「寫字時甚敬，只此是學。」柳氏曰：「運筆在心，心正則筆正。」孰謂藝文之末，非心學之寓也哉？自漢以降，宸翰奎章，代有合作。或用以當顰咲，或寓以代瞽矇，於是紙落人間，重於彝鼎矣。試舉執事所及者：漢光武賜郡國手書，一札十行，皆細書成文，而天下風其節儉；唐文皇賜衛公手墨，大字數幅，皆談兵問疾，而將帥效於鼓鞞；戴至德爲西臺侍郎，而唐高宗手書飛白賜之曰：「汎洪源，侯舟楫。」蓋倚毗之殷也；李至勤御書《千文》，而宋眞宗畋書《孝經》賜之曰：「有資教化，莫若《孝經》。」蓋敦本之致也。之數君者，意非不勤矣，然或玩之以溺志，終非主敬之實心；書非不工矣，然或侈之以競長，終非體物之實學。本之則無，蓋亦藝焉耳已，非眞足以補身心、
translation_en:
… vessels and bowls [reading 盂 for 孟?] was not enough to broaden the mind, and that idle indulgence would inevitably lead to the neglect of learning. Therefore, they would sometimes rest their shoulders in the garden of the arts, or unyoke their carriages by the inkpool; although practicing calligraphy might be said to take away time, doing so was still better than wasting the day altogether. Master Cheng (Cheng Hao 程顥) said: "When writing characters, be utmost in reverence—this very thing is learning." Master Liu (Liu Gongquan 柳公權) said: "Wielding the brush lies in the mind; if the mind is upright, the brush will be upright." Who could say that the minor branches of the literary arts are not a vessel for the learning of the mind?

From the Han dynasty onward, imperial brushwork and sovereign compositions have produced masterworks in every age. Sometimes they were used in place of a frown or a smile [of praise or blame]; sometimes they served as a substitute for the admonitions of the blind musicians. Thus, when a sheet of imperial paper fell into the human realm, it was prized more highly than sacrificial bronzes and tripods. Let me cite the examples mentioned by Your Excellency: Emperor Guangwu of Han (漢光武) bestowed handwritten letters upon the commanderies and princedoms, with ten lines to a single wooden slip, all written in fine script to form complete texts, and the empire was moved by his frugality. Emperor Wen of Tang (唐文皇, i.e., Emperor Taizong) bestowed his own ink brushwork upon the Duke of Wei (Weigong 衛公, Li Jing 李靖)—several scrolls of large characters all discussing military affairs and inquiring after his illness—and his generals and commanders devoted themselves to the war drums. When Dai Zhide (戴至德) served as Vice Director of the Western Terrace (Xitai shilang 西臺侍郎), Emperor Gaozong of Tang (唐高宗) wrote in flying-white script (feibai 飛白) with his own hand and bestowed it upon him, saying: "Crossing the vast waters, I await the boat and oars [reading 俟 for 侯]"—such was the earnestness of his reliance on him. When Li Zhi (李至) earnestly requested [reading 蘄/祈 for 勤?] the imperial calligraphy of the Thousand-Character Classic (Qianwen 千文), Emperor Zhenzong of Song (宋真宗) instead [reading 改 for 畋] wrote out the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiaojing 孝經) and bestowed it upon him, saying: "For aiding moral transformation, nothing compares to the Classic of Filial Piety"—such was the utmost degree of his emphasis on fundamentals.

As for these several sovereigns, their intentions were not lacking in diligence; yet at times they toyed with calligraphy so as to sap their aspirations, which in the end was not the genuine mind of abiding in reverence. Their calligraphy was not lacking in skill; yet at times they flaunted it to compete for superiority, which in the end was not the genuine learning of embodying things. Lacking the fundamental root, it remained merely an art and nothing more—not truly sufficient to benefit body and mind or…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
裨化理也洪惟我
太祖高皇帝當天造草昧之初日進儒臣咨詢
治道於是揭大學衍義於壁間而時爲睇
觀書洪範九疇於座右而
親爲註釋則參前倚衡莫非古訓固不啻與
几筍簴之在御矣乃又
親攄
睿藻製聯句以
賜陶安則謨略文章增輝於漢傑也賦楚辭
===
以
賜宋濂則君臣同樂媲美於卷阿也雖當時
佐命之儔被
寵渥者固不止此而優禮文儒之意尤有獨
至者矣其爲二臣重也豈直家藏飛白之
倫哉我
皇上當天啓文明之會日
御講筵叅決政事於是
書學二帝三王治天下之大經大法於
punctuated: 裨化理也。洪惟我太祖高皇帝當天造草昧之初，日進儒臣，咨詢治道。於是揭《大學衍義》於壁間，而時爲睇觀；書《洪範》九疇於座右，而親爲註釋。則參前倚衡，莫非古訓，固不啻與几筍簴之在御矣。乃又親攄睿藻，製聯句以賜陶安，則謨略文章，增輝於漢傑也；賦《楚辭》以賜宋濂，則君臣同樂，媲美於《卷阿》也。雖當時佐命之儔，被寵渥者固不止此，而優禮文儒之意，尤有獨至者矣。其爲二臣重也，豈直家藏飛白之倫哉！我皇上當天啓文明之會，日御講筵，叅決政事。於是書「學二帝三王治天下之大經大法」於
translation_en:
…and benefit moral transformation and governance.

Reverently reflecting upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), at the initial moment when Heaven was creating order out of chaos, he daily summoned Confucian courtiers to consult them on the way of governance. Thereupon, he posted the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi) upon the walls so as to gaze upon it constantly, and inscribed the Nine Categories of the "Great Plan" (Hongfan) beside his throne, personally composing a commentary for them. Thus, whether standing before him or leaning against his carriage crossbar, there was nothing that was not an ancient precept—truly no less than the inscriptions on stools, armrests, and bell-frames kept in royal use! Moreover, he personally set forth his imperial literary brilliance, composing linked verse to bestow upon Tao An 陶安, whose strategic counsels and literary writings added luster beyond the heroes of the Han; and he composed lyrics in the style of the Songs of Chu (Chuci) to bestow upon Song Lian 宋濂, whereby ruler and minister rejoiced together, matching the beauty of the ode "Curving Slope" (Juan'e). Although among the ranks of founding coadjutors at that time, those who received abundant favor were certainly not limited to these men, his intention of treating literary Confucian scholars with generous courtesy was especially unparalleled here. The honor this conferred upon those two ministers—how could it merely be on a par with families hoarding away "flying-white" calligraphy!

Our August Emperor, meeting a juncture when Heaven has inaugurated civil enlightenment, daily attends the Classics Colloquium and deliberates to decide affairs of state. Thereupon, he inscribed "Study the great standards and great laws by which the Two Emperors and Three Kings governed All-under-Heaven" upon…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
殿額以存顧諟書謹天戒任賢能親賢臣遠
嬖倖明賞罰愼出入愼起居節飲食收放
心存敬畏納忠言撙節用十二事於
宮中以代韋弦則前朝後寢罔非法語之陳
固不啻几席盤盂之在列矣乃又
親灑
宸翰大書徑尺以
賜輔臣有曰汝作舟楫爾惟鹽梅蓋期以商
巖調濟之功也有曰同心夾輔一德和衷
===
蓋望以虞廷協恭之義也雖一時卿侍之
列被
沾灑者亦各有當而尊禮師傅之心尤有獨
先者矣其爲諸臣感也豈直刻石祕書之
比哉要之
聖心精一之所蘊矢口而成言言之所寓者理
也蓋溢乎辭矣
聖心英華之所發肆筆而成書書之所載者道
也蓋進乎藝矣此固上紹乎軒禹湯武之
punctuated: 殿額，以存顧諟；書「謹天戒、任賢能、親賢臣、遠嬖倖、明賞罰、愼出入、愼起居、節飲食、收放心、存敬畏、納忠言、撙節用」十二事於宮中，以代韋弦。則前朝後寢，罔非法語之陳，固不啻几席盤盂之在列矣。乃又親灑宸翰，大書徑尺，以賜輔臣。有曰：「汝作舟楫，爾惟鹽梅」，蓋期以商巖調濟之功也；有曰：「同心夾輔，一德和衷」，蓋望以虞廷協恭之義也。雖一時卿侍之列，被沾灑者亦各有當，而尊禮師傅之心，尤有獨先者矣。其爲諸臣感也，豈直刻石祕書之比哉？要之，聖心精一之所蘊，矢口而成言，言之所寓者理也，蓋溢乎辭矣；聖心英華之所發，肆筆而成書，書之所載者道也，蓋進乎藝矣。此固上紹乎軒、禹、湯、武之
translation_en:
…the palace plaques in order to preserve mindful contemplation; and wrote out in the inner palace the twelve admonitions—"heed the warnings of Heaven, employ the worthy and capable, keep close to worthy ministers, keep sycophants and favorites at a distance, make rewards and punishments clear, be cautious in goings-out and comings-in, be cautious in daily conduct and repose, moderate food and drink, recover the straying mind, maintain reverence and awe, accept loyal counsel, and exercise restraint and economy in expenditures"—to take the place of the soft leather strap and taut bowstring of self-admonition. Thus, in the outer court in front and the residential quarters behind, there is nowhere that exemplary words are not displayed—truly no less than the inscriptions arrayed on armrests, mats, basins, and bowls of old!

Moreover, His Majesty personally wielded the imperial brush, writing large characters a foot across to bestow upon the Grand Secretaries. One inscription reads, "You shall be the boat and oars; you shall be the salt and plum," which is to look to them for the harmonizing and aiding achievements of Fu Yue of the crags of Shang. Another reads, "With united hearts assist on either side; with single virtue harmonize in spirit," which is to hope from them the principle of reverent concord in the court of Shun of Yu. Although those among the ranks of senior officials and close attendants at the time who have received the grace of his brush each received what was fitting, his mind to honor and show courtesy to his tutors and preceptors has taken singular precedence. As for how deeply this moves the ministers, how could it merely be compared to carving inscriptions on stone in the Imperial Library?

In sum, from what is treasured within the pure and unified Sacred Mind, when spoken forth it becomes words, and what dwells within those words is Principle—surpassing mere rhetoric! From the efflorescence emitted by the Sacred Mind, when swept forth from the brush it becomes calligraphy, and what is conveyed in that calligraphy is the Way—advancing beyond mere art! This truly continues on high the transmission of Huangdi, Yu, Tang, and King Wu…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
傳而非近代帝王之所及也執事乃猶欲
攄嘉謨以助
聖修豈臣愚所及乎無亦法祖而已矣詩曰宣
昭義問有虞殷自天言天之當敬也此我
皇上之十二事所以必首夫謹天戒也詩又曰
上天之載無聲無臭儀刑文王萬邦作孚
言天不可知而祖德之所在即天也然則
我
皇上之所以敬天者舍我
===
太祖其安法哉夫其不階尺土而創大業不越
數載而致昇平艱難情僞既已備諳
帝範王猷亦皆洞達宜若可自暇者而乃兢業
益深如我
皇上所謂十二事無一敢忽也試言其實如星
雷變而罪已求言水旱聞而蠲租議賑謹
天戒也弓旌徧訪於巖阿圭組布列於中
外任賢能也朝堂臨決庶政必謀於公卿
親賢臣也內寺供給使令罔干乎事柄遠
punctuated: 傳，而非近代帝王之所及也。執事乃猶欲攄嘉謨以助聖修，豈臣愚所及乎？無亦法祖而已矣。《詩》曰：「宣昭義問，有虞殷自天。」言天之當敬也。此我皇上之十二事，所以必首夫「謹天戒」也。《詩》又曰：「上天之載，無聲無臭。儀刑文王，萬邦作孚。」言天不可知，而祖德之所在即天也。然則我皇上之所以敬天者，舍我太祖其安法哉？夫其不階尺土而創大業，不越數載而致昇平，艱難情僞既已備諳，帝範王猷亦皆洞達，宜若可自暇者，而乃兢業益深，如我皇上所謂十二事，無一敢忽也。試言其實：如星雷變而罪已求言，水旱聞而蠲租議賑，「謹天戒」也；弓旌徧訪於巖阿，圭組布列於中外，「任賢能」也；朝堂臨決，庶政必謀於公卿，「親賢臣」也；內寺供給使令，罔干乎事柄，「遠
translation_en:
… transmission, and is not something that monarchs of recent ages could match. Yet you, the Examiner, still wish to set forth fine counsels to aid His Sacred Cultivation—how could a foolish servant such as I be capable of reaching this?
