Truly, there is nothing else than to take the ancestors as the model.

The Book of Odes (Shijing) says: "Display and make bright your righteous renown, and consider how Yin's mandate came from Heaven." This speaks of how Heaven must be revered. For this reason, among the twelve matters of Our August Emperor, "heeding the warnings of Heaven" must be placed first. The Book of Odes also says: "The workings of High Heaven have neither sound nor scent. Take King Wen (Wen Wang) as your pattern and model, and the myriad states will place their trust in you." This means that Heaven is unknowable, and wherever ancestral virtue resides, that is Heaven. That being so, in seeking the means to revere Heaven, apart from Our Grand Progenitor (Taizu), whom else should Our August Emperor take as his model?

Without relying on a single foot of territory, he founded the great enterprise; within just a few years, he brought about peace and prosperity. Having already thoroughly experienced hardships and human deceit, and having gained penetrating insight into imperial norms and kingly counsels, it might seem he could have allowed himself leisure. Yet his caution and diligence grew ever deeper; with respect to what Our August Emperor calls the twelve matters, there was not a single one that he dared neglect.

Let us try to speak of the actual facts: When anomalies of stars and thunder occurred, he blamed himself and sought frank criticism, and when news of floods or droughts arrived, he remitted taxes and deliberated on relief—this was "heeding the warnings of Heaven." With bows and banners of invitation he sought out men everywhere in mountain recesses, and with jade tablets and official cords he arrayed them in posts within the court and in the provinces—this was "employing the worthy and capable." Holding court in person to decide affairs, he invariably consulted the dukes and ministers on all administrative matters—this was "drawing close to worthy officials." The palace eunuchs were restricted to menial service and running errands, never interfering with the handles of authority—this was "keeping at a distance …

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
嬖倖也薛顯屢立戰功而專擅有罪則封
以侯爵而又謫之海南明賞罰也星存而
出日晡而入動止必占常懷警備慎出入
愼起居也金華進香米則却之太原進葡
萄酒則却之非大宴不設豐饌節飲食也
知人心虛靈乘氣機出入而操存靡怠收
放心也欽畏天地一動一靜儼若神明存
敬畏也廣耳目不偏聽自有位以及芻蕘
咸得叩赤墀而陳説納忠言也無離宮别
===
館之營無奇衺環詭之好無銅山金穴之
賜撙節用也蓋揭廡書壁非徒託之虛文
而潛思力踐無不見之實事此所以創萬
世之安而垂無疆之緒也今我
皇上冲齡踐阼閱歷未深
聖慮憂勤似宜有倍焉者誠以十二事之所戒
而仰質於
太祖之所行一陟一降必奉以周旋一動一言
常恐其判渙則放心自收而同符乎
punctuated: 嬖倖也；薛顯屢立戰功，而專擅有罪，則封以侯爵而又謫之海南，明賞罰也；星存而出，日晡而入，動止必占，常懷警備，慎出入、愼起居也；金華進香米則却之，太原進葡萄酒則却之，非大宴不設豐饌，節飲食也；知人心虛靈，乘氣機出入，而操存靡怠，收放心也；欽畏天地，一動一靜，儼若神明，存敬畏也；廣耳目，不偏聽，自有位以及芻蕘，咸得叩赤墀而陳説，納忠言也；無離宮别館之營，無奇衺環詭之好，無銅山金穴之賜，撙節用也。蓋揭廡書壁，非徒託之虛文；而潛思力踐，無不見之實事，此所以創萬世之安，而垂無疆之緒也。今我皇上冲齡踐阼，閱歷未深，聖慮憂勤，似宜有倍焉者。誠以十二事之所戒，而仰質於太祖之所行，一陟一降，必奉以周旋，一動一言，常恐其判渙，則放心自收而同符乎
translation_en:
…keeping favorites and sycophants at a distance. When Xue Xian 薛顯 repeatedly achieved military merit yet committed the crime of acting arbitrarily on his own authority, he was invested with the title of marquis and yet simultaneously banished to Hainan 海南: this was clarifying rewards and punishments. Going out while the stars were still visible and returning at dusk, divining before every movement and halt, and constantly harboring a sense of vigilance and preparedness: this was being cautious in going out and returning, and being cautious in daily life and repose. When Jinhua 金華 presented fragrant rice, he rejected it; when Taiyuan 太原 presented grape wine, he rejected it; and unless it was a grand banquet, he did not lay out sumptuous delicacies: this was moderating food and drink. Knowing that the human mind is subtle and numinous, moving in and out along with the vital mechanism, and holding fast to it without negligence: this was recovering the straying mind. Revering and standing in awe of Heaven and Earth, in every movement and every moment of stillness as solemn as if before the spirits: this was preserving reverence and awe. Broadening his ears and eyes and refusing to listen partially, so that everyone from officials in office down to grass-cutters and wood-gatherers was able to prostrate himself at the vermilion steps and present his views: this was accepting loyal words. Undertaking no construction of detached palaces or separate lodges, indulging no fondness for strange, perverse, rare, or bizarre things, and bestowing no grants of copper mountains or gold mines: this was economizing on expenditures. Indeed, posting admonitions along the corridors and writing them upon the walls was not merely entrusting them to empty words; rather, through deep reflection and strenuous practice, every single one of them was manifested in actual deeds. This was how he founded ten thousand generations of peace and handed down a boundless patrimony.

Now Our Emperor has ascended the throne at a young age, when his experience of the world is not yet deep, so the anxious diligence of His Sacred Thoughts ought, it seems, to be redoubled. If He truly takes the warnings contained in these twelve matters and reverently measures them against what Grand Progenitor 太祖 put into practice—in every ascent and descent invariably upholding them in His conduct, and in every action and word constantly fearing lest He diverge or become scattered from them—then the straying mind will naturally be recovered and will tally with…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
祖德敬畏自存而克當乎天意二帝三王之大
經大法不俟他求而舟楫鹽梅夾輔和衷
之助亦克有終矣夫然後四海永清而萬
機多暇雖淵嘿無爲以養天和可也雖泳
游翰墨以適天趣亦可也宋儒有言放意
則荒取妍則惑必有事焉神明其德則書
亦有所當敬者宋臣有言願篤志學問皆
如好書益進道德皆如游藝則學又有進
於書者愚敢以是爲
===
今日
獻
第二問
顧憲成
同考試官教諭蔣　批〔考據精詳議論宏博〕
末後條陳我
國家所當修復事宜尤中肯綮他日秉筆直史館可以稱良矣健
羨健羨
同考試官教授黃　批〔史者萬世是非攸係〕
punctuated:
祖德，敬畏自存而克當乎天意。二帝三王之大經大法，不俟他求，而舟楫鹽梅、夾輔和衷之助，亦克有終矣。夫然後四海永清而萬機多暇，雖淵嘿無爲以養天和可也，雖泳游翰墨以適天趣亦可也。宋儒有言：「放意則荒，取妍則惑，必有事焉，神明其德。」則書亦有所當敬者。宋臣有言：「願篤志學問皆如好書，益進道德皆如游藝。」則學又有進於書者。愚敢以是爲今日獻。

第二問
顧憲成
同考試官教諭蔣　批：〔考據精詳，議論宏博。末後條陳我國家所當修復事宜，尤中肯綮。他日秉筆直史館，可以稱良矣。健羨，健羨！〕
同考試官教授黃　批：〔史者，萬世是非攸係，〕
translation_en:
…the virtue of the Imperial Ancestors; reverence and awe will naturally abide, and He will be able to answer to the will of Heaven. The great norms and great laws of the Two Emperors and Three Kings will not need to be sought elsewhere, and the assistance of those who serve as boats and oars or salt and plum—assisting in harmony of heart—will also be brought to a successful conclusion. Only then, when the Four Seas are forever tranquil and there is ample leisure amid the myriad affairs of state, even if He remains in deep silence and non-action to nourish heavenly harmony, it will be permissible; and even if He swims and wanders in brush and ink to suit His natural inclinations, it will also be permissible. A Song Confucian scholar once said: "If one lets one's mind run loose, one becomes careless; if one seeks mere beauty, one becomes deluded; one must always be intent upon the task, illuminating one's virtue like a spirit." Thus calligraphy too is something toward which one ought to maintain reverence. A Song minister once said: "I wish that Your Majesty would devote Your will to learning just as You love calligraphy, and ever advance in morality just as You dabble in the arts." Thus learning goes even further beyond calligraphy. In my simplicity, I dare to offer this for the present day.

Question 2
Gu Xiancheng 顧憲成
Associate Examiner and Instructor Jiang 蔣 comments: 〔The evidentiary research is precise and detailed, and the argumentation is vast and wide-ranging. At the end, his itemized presentation of the matters that our State ought to restore and revive especially hits the crucial points. In days to come, when he holds the brush on duty in the Historiography Institute, he may well be called a fine historian! Truly admirable, truly admirable!〕
Associate Examiner and Instructor Huang 黃 comments: 〔History is that upon which the right and wrong of ten thousand generations depend,…〕

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
因以亟觀鑒而昭勸戒且
朝寧舉措亦藉此爲自省之助顧職之者誠難此策條悉歷代廢
興與我
今日所當脩復者議尤詳悉非陳言無補者比也異日敷對
大廷商確時事子奚讓焉宜錄之以式
考試官右贊善陳　批　條荅史職廢興明切可誦
有考據有規畫末復寓忠讜于言表宜錄
考試官左中允戴　批　歷代史職廢興條對詳核
而結意深寓規諷足見靖獻之志矣
===
甚哉史之難言也非史之難能稱其職之
難也非吾稱之難所以使之能稱其職之
難也夫史者權衡是非贊揚治理一日不
可廢矣顧微文刺譏挺言糾過則見以爲
訕華語崇褒腓辭餙關則見以爲僞此何
以稱焉遡稽往古史職之興也則在明良
交會之朝而廢也嘗于上下猜疑之日何
者時當至治顯讃鴻業史不勝書若此者
非溢美也藉以爲鑒也而君德以之益修
punctuated:
因以亟觀鑒而昭勸戒，且朝寧舉措，亦藉此爲自省之助，顧職之者誠難。此策條悉歷代廢興，與我今日所當脩復者，議尤詳悉，非陳言無補者比也。異日敷對大廷，商確時事，子奚讓焉？宜錄之以式。
考試官右贊善陳　批：條荅史職廢興，明切可誦，有考據，有規畫，末復寓忠讜于言表，宜錄。
考試官左中允戴　批：歷代史職廢興，條對詳核，而結意深寓規諷，足見靖獻之志矣。
甚哉，史之難言也！非史之難，能稱其職之難也；非吾稱之難，所以使之能稱其職之難也。夫史者，權衡是非，贊揚治理，一日不可廢矣。顧微文刺譏，挺言糾過，則見以爲訕；華語崇褒，腓辭餙關，則見以爲僞。此何以稱焉？遡稽往古，史職之興也，則在明良交會之朝；而廢也，嘗于上下猜疑之日。何者？時當至治，顯讃鴻業，史不勝書。若此者，非溢美也，藉以爲鑒也；而君德以之益修，
translation_en:
…whereby one may urgently draw lessons for reflection and make clear encouragement and warning. Moreover, the measures taken by the Court also rely on this as an aid to self-examination, though those who hold the office find it truly difficult. This policy essay sets forth item by item its rise and decline through successive dynasties, and as for what we ought to restore today, its discussion is especially detailed and thorough—not to be compared with stale words that are of no help. On a future day, when you present your reply in the Great Court and deliberate upon current affairs, why should you yield to anyone? It should be recorded as a model.

Examiner Chen, Right Admonisher (you zanshan), comments: Its itemized answers regarding the rise and decline of the historiographical office are clear, incisive, and worthy of recitation. It has both evidentiary scholarship and practical planning, and at the end it further conveys loyal and forthright counsel beyond the surface of the words. It should be recorded.

Examiner Dai, Left Companion (zuo zhongyun), comments: The rise and decline of the historiographical office through successive dynasties is answered item by item with detail and accuracy, and the concluding thought deeply embodies admonition and remonstrance, which suffices to show his resolve for devoted service to the sovereign.

How extreme is the difficulty of speaking of history! Yet it is not history itself that is difficult, but being able to fulfill the duties of its office that is difficult; and it is not our fulfilling those duties that is difficult, but that whereby one is enabled to fulfill the duties of the office that is difficult. Now history weighs right and wrong and praises and exalts the principles of governance; it cannot be dispensed with for a single day. Yet if one uses subtle phrasing to criticize and satirize, or speaks out forthrightly to correct faults, it is regarded as slander; if one uses ornate language to lavish praise, or servile words [?] to gloss over flaws [?], it is regarded as falsity. How then can the office be fulfilled? Tracing back and examining antiquity, when the office of the historian flourished, it was in courts where enlightened rulers and worthy ministers met in harmony; and when it fell into disuse, it was ever in days of mutual suspicion between above and below. Why is this? When the times are at the height of supreme order, great achievements are manifestly praised, and the historians have more to record than they can write down. Such writings are not excessive flattery; they are relied upon as a mirror, and through them the ruler's virtue is ever more cultivated,…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
治道以之益振矣世際陵夷涖德靡政史
不勝書不然者則諛詞也懼其賈禍也而
君德以之日昏治道以之日替矣職有廢
興而善敗昭治亂判焉迺可不慎歟邇者
詔復起居史職誠千載一時也愚生墨守章句
未窺承明著作之庭而執事舉以策士敢
無詞以復蓋聞之有一時之榮辱有萬世
之榮辱爵賞刑威一時之榮辱也其權總
于人主簡冊紀載萬世之榮辱也其事責
===
之史官然刑賞失實不過爽一時之勸懲
紀錄失實則將攺萬世之觀聽史職所繫
顧不重邪是故先王之世朝有二史以司
言動言則左史書之動則右史書之在周
官者可睹也惟職司言動凡上自王朝下
逮士庶臧否成敗咸謹書備錄昭示無極
夫美惡之號不隱洺故實者可稽得失之
載具明徵往事者可鏡君無過舉臣無回
守恒必繇之矣嘗考之古焉孔甲盤盂藏
punctuated:
治道以之益振矣。世際陵夷，涖德靡政，史不勝書；不然者，則諛詞也，懼其賈禍也，而君德以之日昏，治道以之日替矣。職有廢興，而善敗昭、治亂判焉，迺可不慎歟？邇者詔復起居史職，誠千載一時也。愚生墨守章句，未窺承明著作之庭，而執事舉以策士，敢無詞以復？

蓋聞之：有一時之榮辱，有萬世之榮辱。爵賞刑威，一時之榮辱也，其權總于人主；簡冊紀載，萬世之榮辱也，其事責之史官。然刑賞失實，不過爽一時之勸懲；紀錄失實，則將攺萬世之觀聽。史職所繫，顧不重邪？是故先王之世，朝有二史以司言動：言則左史書之，動則右史書之，在《周官》者可睹也。惟職司言動，凡上自王朝，下逮士庶，臧否成敗，咸謹書備錄，昭示無極。夫美惡之號不隱，洺故實者可稽；得失之載具明，徵往事者可鏡。君無過舉，臣無回守，恒必繇之矣。嘗考之古焉：孔甲《盤盂》藏
translation_en:
… and the way of governance is thereby ever more invigorated. When an age encounters decline, perverse virtue [?] and decadent administration are more than the historians can finish recording; or if not so, then what is written is mere flattery out of fear of courting disaster, whereby the sovereign's virtue grows daily more benighted and the way of governance daily deteriorates. As the historiographical office flourishes or falls into disuse, success and failure are made manifest and order and disorder are distinguished—how then could one not treat it with caution? Recently, an imperial decree restored the historiographical office of the Diaries of Activity and Repose, which is truly the opportunity of a thousand years. Though a foolish student like myself merely clings to chapter and phrase and has never glimpsed the Court of Literary Composition in the Hall of Resplendent Brilliance (Chengming), since Your Excellency has raised this in a policy question to test the candidates, how dare I not offer words in reply?

I have heard that there is the honor and disgrace of a single moment, and there is the honor and disgrace of ten thousand generations. Ranks and rewards, punishments and awe are the honor and disgrace of a single moment, and their authority is gathered in the hands of the ruler; records on bamboo slips and in books are the honor and disgrace of ten thousand generations, and their responsibility is charged to the historiography officials. Yet when punishments and rewards miss the truth, it does no more than disrupt encouragement and warning for a single moment; whereas when historical records miss the truth, it alters what ten thousand generations see and hear. Is what hinges upon the office of the historian not weighty indeed? Therefore, in the age of the former kings, the court had two historians to take charge of words and actions: words were written down by the Historian of the Left, and actions were written down by the Historian of the Right, as can be seen in the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan). Because their office was in charge of words and actions, everything from the royal court above down to thegentlemen and commoners below—good and bad, success and failure—was carefully written and fully recorded, to be clearly displayed without end. When designations of noble and base are not concealed, those who inquire into [?] historical precedents can verify them; when records of success and failure are completely clear, those who seek evidence from past affairs can take them as a mirror. That the sovereign makes no errant moves and the ministers harbor no devious conduct has always depended on this. I have examined antiquity on this point: the Inscriptions on Basins and Bowls (Panyu) of Kong Jia were stored…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
在冊府而金縢史祝非弁風雷啓變雖聖召
不得與聞古史之密如此以故法戒烱然
而垂世不磨耳後之論史者吾惑之柳蚪
欲當朝顯言其狀後付史館不知史者關
後來之遠鑒非止張一時之公論況不能
顯言者其何以昭直筆乎李昉欲先奏御
後付有司不知史者非徒表善以彰美寔
欲紀過以垂戒儻有不敢不諱者幾何而
不爲諛書乎夫任天下萬世之事宜以天
===
下萬世之心處之故據事直書猶懼不足
以示鑑況迂其辭以諱其寔天下後世其
誰信之蚪與昉之論非史之訓矣漢武帝
設禁中起居而太史公位在丞相上制亦
重矣然當時筭商告緡猶故也征伐禱祀
猶故也史果足爲鑑乎未幾龍門腐刑蓋
欲滅史籍而非專爲李陵也漢之史可知
矣唐初以給諫兼知起居每仗下議事起
居郎執簡紀錄立法善矣然當時禁門喋
punctuated: 在冊府，而《金縢》史祝，非弁風雷啓變，雖聖召不得與聞。古史之密如此，以故法戒烱然，而垂世不磨耳。後之論史者，吾惑之。柳蚪欲當朝顯言其狀，後付史館，不知史者關後來之遠鑒，非止張一時之公論，況不能顯言者，其何以昭直筆乎？李昉欲先奏御，後付有司，不知史者非徒表善以彰美，寔欲紀過以垂戒，儻有不敢不諱者，幾何而不爲諛書乎？夫任天下萬世之事，宜以天下萬世之心處之。故據事直書，猶懼不足以示鑑，況迂其辭以諱其寔，天下後世其誰信之？蚪與昉之論，非史之訓矣。漢武帝設禁中起居，而太史公位在丞相上，制亦重矣。然當時筭商告緡猶故也，征伐禱祀猶故也，史果足爲鑑乎？未幾，龍門腐刑，蓋欲滅史籍，而非專爲李陵也，漢之史可知矣。唐初以給諫兼知起居，每仗下議事，起居郎執簡紀錄，立法善矣。然當時禁門喋
translation_en: … were kept in the palace archives, and as for the scribe's prayer in the Metal-Bound Coffer (Jinteng), had the capped king [King Cheng] not opened it upon the portent of wind and thunder, even the sage Duke of Shao would not have been privy to it. Such was the confidentiality of ancient historiographers; for this reason, models and warnings shone brightly and were handed down through the ages without being effaced. As for those in later times who discussed historiography, I am perplexed by them. Liu Qiu 柳蚪 wanted matters to be openly stated at court first and only afterward handed over to the Historiography Institute, not realizing that history concerns the distant mirror of posterity and does not merely advance the public opinion of a single moment; moreover, for matters that cannot be openly stated, how could straight writing be made manifest? Li Fang 李昉 wanted records to be presented to the throne first and afterward handed over to the authorities, not realizing that history is not merely for displaying goodness to highlight beauty, but truly seeks to record faults in order to hand down warnings; if there are things one dares not fail to taboo, how far would that be from becoming a work of flattery? Now, in undertaking the affairs of the world and ten thousand generations, one ought to handle them with the mind of the world and ten thousand generations. Therefore, even when writing straightforwardly according to the facts, one still fears it is insufficient to serve as a mirror; how much more so when one makes the wording circuitous in order to conceal the reality—who in the world and in later generations will believe it? The arguments of Qiu and Fang are not the teachings of historiography. Emperor Wu of Han established the Court Diaries of the Forbidden Palace, and the Grand Scribe (Taishigong) ranked above the Counselor-in-Chief; the institution was weighty indeed. Yet at that time, the taxing of merchants and confiscation of unassessed property strings went on as before, and military campaigns and prayers and sacrifices went on as before—did history truly suffice to serve as a mirror? Before long, the historian of Longmen [Sima Qian 司馬遷] suffered the punishment of castration, which was doubtless out of a desire to obliterate historical records and not solely because of Li Ling 李陵; the state of historiography in the Han can thus be known. At the beginning of the Tang, Supervising Secretaries and Remonstrators concurrently took charge of the Court Diaries; whenever affairs were deliberated after the ceremonial guards retired, the Imperial Diarist (Qijulang) held his tablets to record them—the law as established was fine indeed. Yet at that time, the wading in [blood] at the palace gates …

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
血不諱也帷簿貽羞不諱也史果可爲鑑
乎至永徽間宰相奏請多畏人知而文宗
欲自觀史唐之史可知矣宋以宰相監脩
學士修撰又兩府記政三館之士注起居
總而論之書搨前議論有時政記錄柱下
見聞有起居注書經筵言動有邇英延義
記注類而次之謂日曆修而成之謂寔錄
制亦詳矣然員具而象闕未嘗廢職而著
作無當其所撰述特據供報故事闕大體
===
史官欲書而不得撰述既成錄本進御故
事多避諱史官能書而不敢如歐陽脩所
議者安在其爲史哉隆興中胡銓奏記注
之失有四一進史不當二立非其地三前
殿不立四奏不直前夫奏御侍立歐陽脩
言之矣宋初史官直前奏事朝政與議有
史諫之意嗣後不預牒不奏不列班不奏
而直前之議遂寢此銓所爲嘆惜也汪藻
脩日曆欲設四類以求之一年表二官閥
punctuated: 血，不諱也；帷簿貽羞，不諱也。史果可爲鑑乎？至永徽間，宰相奏請多畏人知，而文宗欲自觀史，唐之史可知矣。宋以宰相監脩，學士修撰，又兩府記政，三館之士注起居。總而論之，書搨前議論有時政記，錄柱下見聞有起居注，書經筵言動有邇英、延義記注；類而次之謂日曆，修而成之謂寔錄，制亦詳矣。然員具而象闕，未嘗廢職而著作無當。其所撰述特據供報，故事闕大體，史官欲書而不得；撰述既成，錄本進御，故事多避諱，史官能書而不敢，如歐陽脩所議者，安在其爲史哉！隆興中，胡銓奏記注之失有四：一、進史不當；二、立非其地；三、前殿不立；四、奏不直前。夫奏御、侍立，歐陽脩言之矣。宋初史官直前奏事，朝政與議，有史諫之意。嗣後不預牒不奏，不列班不奏，而直前之議遂寢，此銓所爲嘆惜也。汪藻脩日曆，欲設四類以求之：一、年表；二、官閥；
translation_en:
… bloodshed [at the palace gates], they had no scruples against it; bringing disgrace upon the inner quarters, they had no scruples against it. Could history truly serve as a mirror? By the Yonghui era (650–655), when the Grand Councilors submitted memorials and requests, they mostly feared that others would know of them, and Emperor Wenzong (r. 827–840) wished to inspect the historical records himself; from this, the state of history in the Tang can be known.

In the Song, Grand Councilors served as Superintendents of Compilation, and Academicians served as Compilers; furthermore, the Two Administrations recorded governmental affairs, and scholars of the Three Institutes kept the Imperial Diary. To speak of it in sum: for writing down discussions before the imperial couch there were the Records of Current Government (Shizheng ji); for recording what was seen and heard beneath the pillars there were the Imperial Diaries (Qiju zhu); for writing down words and deeds at the Classics Colloquium there were the Diary Annotations of the Eryi and Yanyi Halls. Classifying and ordering these was called the Daily Calendar (Rili), and compiling them into final form was called the Veritable Records (Shilu). The institution was indeed detailed! Yet while the personnel were all in place, the true spirit was lacking; the offices were never abolished, yet their compositions were inadequate. Because what they compiled was based merely on routine reports supplied to them, affairs lacked the grand essentials, and when the Historiographers wished to write, they had no way to obtain the facts; and once a compilation was finished, a transcribed copy was presented to the throne, so that in many affairs they avoided taboos, and though the Historiographers were able to write, they did not dare to—just as Ouyang Xiu 歐陽脩 criticized. Wherein, then, did its nature as history lie?

During the Longxing era (1163–1164), Hu Quan 胡銓 memorialized that there were four failings in the keeping of the court diaries: first, presenting the histories to the throne was improper; second, the diarists stood in the wrong place; third, they did not stand in attendance in the front palace hall; and fourth, they did not memorialize directly before the throne. Now, as for presenting records to the Emperor and standing in attendance, Ouyang Xiu had already spoken of these. At the beginning of the Song, Historiographers stepped directly before the throne to memorialize on affairs and participated in discussions of court governance, which embodied the principle of remonstrance through history. Thereafter, if they did not give advance notice by official dispatch they could not memorialize, and if they were not in the regular court ranks they could not memorialize; thus the practice of deliberation directly before the throne was discontinued, which is what Hu Quan lamented. When Wang Zao 汪藻 compiled the Daily Calendar, he wished to establish four categories by which to seek out materials: first, chronological tables; second, official careers and lineages; …

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
三政迹四凡例蓋歲爲旁通以定時日人
爲纍歷以傳始終事爲源流以稽始末至
謂有一月之例一季之例一年三年之例
亦脩史者所不廢也總而論之三代以上
是非之權直寄于史官故世有良史三代
以下是非之權陰陽于人主故史鮮直筆
創業之主憂勤惕厲欲子孫知締造之艱
難故其政多美而史也恒詳守成之主後
汏易生恐貽譏于汗簡故其政多疵而史
也嘗諱則其大較也已我
===
明稽古爲治慎重是任嘗考
高皇帝定鼎之初卽設起居注而以宋濂輩充
之日侍
帷幄卽周置左右史遺意也漢唐宋莫能及
矣後易爲修撰等官列屬翰院以紀載事
重故設官加詳非所罷廢自職名更定之
後遂謂
累朝史文闕略而言者屢爲請矣今
punctuated: 三、政迹，四、凡例。蓋歲爲旁通以定時日，人爲纍歷以傳始終，事爲源流以稽始末；至謂有一月之例、一季之例、一年三年之例，亦脩史者所不廢也。總而論之：三代以上，是非之權直寄于史官，故世有良史；三代以下，是非之權陰陽于人主，故史鮮直筆。創業之主，憂勤惕厲，欲子孫知締造之艱難，故其政多美，而史也恒詳；守成之主，後汏易生，恐貽譏于汗簡，故其政多疵，而史也嘗諱，則其大較也已。我明稽古爲治，慎重是任。嘗考高皇帝定鼎之初，卽設起居注，而以宋濂輩充之，日侍帷幄，卽周置左右史遺意也，漢、唐、宋莫能及矣。後易爲修撰等官，列屬翰院，以紀載事重，故設官加詳，非所罷廢。自職名更定之後，遂謂累朝史文闕略，而言者屢爲請矣。今
translation_en:
… third, administrative deeds; and fourth, general principles of compilation. For the years are arranged in cross-referenced tables to fix the dates; individuals are given cumulative service records to transmit their careers from beginning to end; and events are traced by their origins and developments to examine their whole course from start to finish. As for his speaking of monthly precedents, seasonal precedents, and annual or triennial precedents, these too are things that compilers of history do not discard.

To sum it up and discuss it as a whole: In the Three Dynasties and earlier, the authority to judge right and wrong was entrusted directly to the court historians, and therefore the world had fine historians. After the Three Dynasties, the authority to judge right and wrong was subtly manipulated by the ruler, and therefore histories rarely had forthright brushes. Founding rulers were anxious, diligent, vigilant, and circumspect, wishing their descendants to know the hardships of establishing the state; thus their governance had many admirable qualities, and the histories were consistently detailed. Rulers who merely maintained the heritage easily gave way to extravagance [reading 侈/汰 for 後汏?] and feared leaving behind ridicule in the historical records; thus their governance had many flaws, and the histories regularly practiced taboo and concealment. Such is the general pattern.

Our Ming dynasty examines antiquity in governing and treats this responsibility with great prudence. I have noted that when the High Emperor (Gao Huangdi) first established the dynasty, he immediately instituted Diaries of Activity and Repose (Qijuzhu) and appointed men such as Song Lian 宋濂 to serve as Court Diarists, waiting daily within the imperial tent—which was precisely the inherited intent of the Zhou dynasty in establishing the Historians of the Left and Right, something that the Han, Tang, and Song could not match. Later, these posts were changed into Senior Compilers (Xiuzhuan) and other officials, arrayed under the Hanlin Academy. Because the matter of historical recording was weighty, the establishment of offices was made more detailed; it was not that the function was abolished or abandoned. Yet after the official titles were changed and reset, people consequently claimed that the historical records of successive reigns were defective and sketchy, and critics repeatedly submitted requests concerning this. Now, the present…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
上聰明馭極百度聿新頃
俞輔臣之請令史官知起居注仰稽
成憲忝酌時宜寖詳且善此
大聖之遠舉
熙朝之極事矣愚將何以爲獻乎伏覩今
上朝講不輟盛德也躬親
大祀至仁也信任元輔至明也
臨雍重道大典也奉事
兩宮純孝也苞舉藝文
===
上春也四年之間
嘉言懿政煌煌哉難縷述焉至其
御平臺親計吏親銓選此數端者皆最高前
古之事而
上冲齡始政毅然舉之繇此日臨羣臣日明習
國家事
聖智愈光有史不絕書者矣議者猶謂
法宮嚴邃非外庭疏遠與聞
朝政萬幾非一時闕訪能悉此豈過計而迂
punctuated: 上聰明馭極，百度聿新，頃俞輔臣之請，令史官知起居注，仰稽成憲，忝酌時宜，寖詳且善。此大聖之遠舉，熙朝之極事矣，愚將何以爲獻乎？伏覩今上朝講不輟，盛德也；躬親大祀，至仁也；信任元輔，至明也；臨雍重道，大典也；奉事兩宮，純孝也；苞舉藝文，上春也。四年之間，嘉言懿政，煌煌哉！難縷述焉。至其御平臺，親計吏，親銓選，此數端者，皆最高前古之事，而上冲齡始政，毅然舉之。繇此日臨羣臣，日明習國家事，聖智愈光，有史不絕書者矣。議者猶謂法宮嚴邃，非外庭疏遠與聞；朝政萬幾，非一時闕訪能悉。此豈過計而迂
translation_en:
…the present Emperor guides the realm with intelligence and wisdom, renewing all institutions. Recently, He approved the request of the Grand Secretaries and ordered the Historiographers to serve as Imperial Diarists, looking up to examine the established statutes while deliberating upon what is appropriate for the times, making the system increasingly detailed and perfected. This is a far-reaching initiative of a Great Sage and the supreme achievement of a flourishing dynasty! What then can I, in my ignorance, offer by way of counsel?

I humbly observe that the present Emperor holds court and attends the Classics Mat lectures without cease—this is abundant virtue; He personally performs the Great Sacrifices—this is utmost benevolence; He places trust in the Senior Grand Secretary—this is utmost discernment; He visits the Imperial Academy to honor the Way—this is a grand canon; He serves the Two Empresses Dowager—this is pure filial piety; He encompasses and cultivates literature and the arts—this is lofty [?] [上春; possibly a transcription error for 至善, supreme goodness, or 至文, supreme culture]. Within the span of four years, how brilliant have been His admirable words and exemplary governance! They are too numerous to recount in detail. As for His giving audience at the Pingtai (Platform of Equitable Governance), personally conducting the Great Reckoning of officials, and personally overseeing civil service appointments—these several matters are all deeds that surpass remotest antiquity, yet the Emperor, beginning His rule at a young age, has resolutely carried them out. Through this, He daily meets His assembled ministers and daily grows more conversant with the affairs of state; His sacred wisdom shines ever brighter, such that the scribes never cease recording it.

Yet commentators still say that the Forbidden Palace is solemn and secluded, so that distant officials of the outer court cannot hear of what transpires within; and that the myriad affairs of court governance cannot all be fully known through occasional inquiries into omissions. Is this merely excessive worry and impractical…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
說邪今之
詔旨批答
殿庭宣御顯然載冊籍矣若
燕閒蠖濩之間能無
睿想德音爲臣民莊誦者乎不得而睹矣府部
議覆疏牘陳請燦然收館局矣但時政沿
革之故豈無秘謨隱狀非議疏槩見者乎
不得而核矣况事以時移則尋繹鮮據見
隨人異則軒輊莫憑跡涉風聞則疑似互
===
執情託微渺則鈎賾無端嗟乎勢必至此
矣曩時史職未飭尚可諉也今職掌所裁
定甚明矣異日者儻一言詿誤一事漏佚
何所逃責邪愚竊有說焉講官記注起居
即宋邇英延義意也然大臣
宣對不常盛典未備况事機有難外泄者則
造膝密語誰其効之請自文華
講讀外不時召見政務人才咸與商確使從
容獻替
punctuated: 說邪？今之詔旨批答、殿庭宣御，顯然載冊籍矣；若燕閒蠖濩之間，能無睿想德音為臣民莊誦者乎？不得而睹矣。府部議覆、疏牘陳請，燦然收館局矣；但時政沿革之故，豈無秘謨隱狀非議疏槩見者乎？不得而核矣。况事以時移，則尋繹鮮據；見隨人異，則軒輊莫憑；跡涉風聞，則疑似互執；情託微渺，則鈎賾無端。嗟乎！勢必至此矣。曩時史職未飭，尚可諉也；今職掌所裁定甚明矣，異日者儻一言詿誤、一事漏佚，何所逃責邪？愚竊有說焉：講官記注起居，即宋邇英、延義意也。然大臣宣對不常，盛典未備；况事機有難外泄者，則造膝密語，誰其効之？請自文華講讀外，不時召見，政務、人才咸與商確，使從容獻替，
translation_en: … argument? Today's imperial edicts and rescript responses, as well as pronouncements and audiences in the palace halls, are clearly recorded in the official registers. Yet during moments of private leisure within the secluded palace apartments, could there not be sagely reflections and virtuous words worthy of being reverently recited by officials and the people? These cannot be witnessed. The deliberative replies of the Chief Military Commissions and the Six Ministries, along with memorials setting forth requests, are brilliantly collected in the Historiography Institute. However, regarding the reasons behind the continuities and changes in current governance, how could there not be confidential counsels and hidden circumstances that are not fully revealed in the deliberative memorials? These cannot be verified. Moreover, as events shift over time, tracing their threads leaves little solid evidence; as views vary from person to person, there is no reliable basis for weighing relative merits; when traces of events rest on hearsay, doubts and conjectures are mutually insisted upon; and when circumstances are veiled in subtlety and obscurity, probing into the depths has no starting point. Alas! Circumstances must inevitably come to this. In the past, when historiographical duties were not yet strictly regulated, one could still make excuses; now, what has been established for these official duties is exceedingly clear. If on a future day a single word is erroneous or a single matter is omitted, how could one escape blame? I humbly have a proposal: having the Lecturers record the Imperial Diary is precisely the intent of the Eying and Yanyi halls of the Song dynasty. Yet because high ministers are not summoned for audiences regularly, this grand institution remains incomplete; furthermore, when matters of state involve crucial secrets difficult to disclose to the outside, who then will offer intimate, knee-to-knee counsel? I beg that, apart from the lectures and readings at the Wenhua Hall, Your Majesty grant frequent and unscheduled audiences to deliberate thoroughly with them on both state affairs and human talent, allowing them unhurriedly to offer counsel on what to adopt and what to reject, …

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
垂聽而施行之書之史氏琬琰增輝矣况又
先朝已試之効乎是故
宣對宜勤也分曹紀錄有專職矣惟按諸司
供報耳如書吏部陞黜某官不聞功罪何
若其他錢穀甲兵禮刑營務諸類委曲寧
盡知邪請擇文學司官專知其事即以日
記堂稿一一據實以報史官仍悉心博訪
不獨紀事并情狀得之使後來讀者如親
睹其事乃不大舛訛耳是故考核宜詳也
古史如諸志表傳皆遷固諸人檃括時事
===
以成自
實錄專行紀志殆廢亦史家缺典也遂使創
置典禮諸重大之事非片言能具者亦散
入紀年能無複語贅書乎若於一事終始
預令聯絡其辭首尾貫串仿古傳記爲之
寧詳毋略佗日纂修採掇尤便矣古列國
有史掌記時事采風而獻之王朝今諸省
遐州僻邑其間孝子弟弟順孫貞婦及災
punctuated: 垂聽而施行之，書之史氏，琬琰增輝矣，况又先朝已試之効乎？是故宣對宜勤也。分曹紀錄，有專職矣，惟按諸司供報耳。如書吏部陞黜某官，不聞功罪何若；其他錢穀、甲兵、禮刑、營務諸類委曲，寧盡知邪？請擇文學司官專知其事，即以日記、堂稿一一據實以報；史官仍悉心博訪，不獨紀事，并情狀得之，使後來讀者如親睹其事，乃不大舛訛耳。是故考核宜詳也。古史如諸志、表、傳，皆遷、固諸人檃括時事以成。自實錄專行，紀、志殆廢，亦史家缺典也。遂使創置、典禮諸重大之事，非片言能具者，亦散入紀年，能無複語贅書乎？若於一事終始，預令聯絡其辭，首尾貫串，仿古傳記爲之，寧詳毋略，佗日纂修採掇尤便矣。古列國有史，掌記時事，采風而獻之王朝。今諸省遐州僻邑，其間孝子、弟弟、順孫、貞婦，及災
translation_en:
… should graciously listen and put it into practice. When recorded by the historiographers, it will add luster to the jade tablets of history—especially since this has already proven effective under previous reigns! Therefore, imperial audiences and consultations ought to be frequent.

Although the division of bureaus for recording history now has dedicated assignments, they merely rely on the reports submitted by the various offices. For instance, when recording that the Ministry of Personnel promoted or demoted a certain official, one hears nothing of what his merits or offenses actually were; as for the intricate details of other matters such as revenue and grain, armor and weaponry, rites and punishments, or construction works, how could they possibly know them all? I beg that erudite bureau officials be selected to take special charge of these matters, reporting everything truthfully item by item based on daily records and ministerial drafts. The historiographers should still make exhaustive and wide-ranging inquiries of their own, capturing not only the events themselves but also their underlying circumstances, so that future readers will feel as though they are witnessing the events firsthand, and only then will there be no gross errors or discrepancies. Therefore, investigation and verification ought to be thorough.

In ancient histories, the various treatises, tables, and biographies were all completed by men such as Sima Qian 司馬遷 and Ban Gu 班固 by reshaping and synthesizing contemporary affairs. Ever since the Veritable Records (Shilu) became the sole format in use, basic annals and treatises have been virtually abandoned, which is likewise a deficiency in historiography. Consequently, major affairs such as institutional foundations and state rituals, which cannot be fully conveyed in a few words, are also scattered across the chronological entries—how could this avoid repetitive language and redundant writing? If, for the entirety of a single affair from beginning to end, the wording is arranged in advance to connect smoothly and run coherently from start to finish in imitation of ancient biographical and narrative accounts—erring on the side of detail rather than brevity—it will be especially convenient for selection and compilation when the history is edited in the future.

In antiquity, the various feudal states had scribes in charge of recording contemporary affairs, collecting local customs, and presenting them to the royal court. Today, in the distant prefectures and isolated districts of the various provinces, the filial sons, fraternal younger brothers, obedient grandsons, chaste wives, as well as calamities…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
祥風俗諸所沿廢之類湮滅不傳者亡限
也請責成督學官所在徧訪歲終類報以
備考訂庶隱行微跡不格于
上聞矣雖然凡兹所陳亦須緣史職更定謬効
其愚若此耳大都迂疎之見無能裨史事
萬一者然帝王所以恢鴻業而垂芳規者
豈惟其一掌書一列史之爲兢兢哉夫亦
蓄德論道而令終之是圖也往古之君其
朝未嘗無載筆執簡之臣也其側未嘗無
===
記注垂戒之書也然而不隆于治焉此亡
佗以虛員徒備而實鑑不存耳假令備員
而無取于鑑則史無異乎路說而官無異
乎木主也即董狐南史安所稱良哉是故
纂猷述烈以勅今昔之訓者古史之大義
也端本澄源以鑒聖哲之規者
明后之偉節也異時蘭臺麟閣之彥且頌盛美
而難爲詞矣草莽愚生拭目望焉
第三問
punctuated:
祥、風俗、諸所沿廢之類，湮滅不傳者，亡限也。請責成督學官，所在徧訪，歲終類報，以備考訂，庶隱行微跡不格于上聞矣。雖然，凡兹所陳，亦須緣史職更定，謬効其愚若此耳。大都迂疎之見，無能裨史事萬一者。然帝王所以恢鴻業而垂芳規者，豈惟其一掌書、一列史之爲兢兢哉？夫亦蓄德論道而令終之是圖也。往古之君，其朝未嘗無載筆執簡之臣也，其側未嘗無記注垂戒之書也，然而不隆于治焉。此亡佗，以虛員徒備而實鑑不存耳。假令備員而無取于鑑，則史無異乎路說，而官無異乎木主也。即董狐、南史，安所稱良哉？是故纂猷述烈，以勅今昔之訓者，古史之大義也；端本澄源，以鑒聖哲之規者，明后之偉節也。異時蘭臺、麟閣之彥，且頌盛美而難爲詞矣。草莽愚生，拭目望焉。

第三問
translation_en:
…portents, local customs, and the various institutions continued or abolished that have sunk into oblivion and gone unrecorded are limitless. I beg that the Education Intendants be charged with making thorough inquiries in their jurisdictions and submitting classified reports at the end of each year to be kept for reference and verification, so that hidden deeds and obscure traces will not be barred from reaching His Majesty's hearing. Even so, all that I have set forth here merely follows upon the reorganization of the historiographical offices in ventured offering of my humble folly. For the most part, these are impractical and superficial views, incapable of benefiting historiographical affairs by even one part in ten thousand. Yet whereby emperors and kings expand their great enterprise and hand down fragrant models to posterity—how could it merely be a matter of cautious concern over a single archivist or a single line of historians? Rather, it lies in accumulating virtue, discoursing on the Way, and planning for a noble consummation. Among the rulers of antiquity, their courts were never without ministers carrying brushes and holding tablets, and their sides were never without diaries of activity and books of admonition; and yet some did not achieve prosperity in governance. This was for no other reason than that nominal posts were merely filled in vain while genuine reflection in the mirror of history did not exist. Supposing that one fills the posts of historians without drawing lessons from their mirror, then histories are no different from street gossip, and historians are no different from wooden ancestral tablets! Even if one had a Dong Hu or a Historian Nan (Nanshi), wherein would they be praised as good historians? Therefore, to compile plans and recount meritorious deeds so as to set in order the lessons of past and present is the great principle of ancient history; to rectify the root and purify the source so as to take the models of sages and worthies as a mirror is the magnificent conduct of an enlightened sovereign. On a future day, the outstanding talents of the Orchid Terrace and Unicorn Pavilion will praise His Majesty's flourishing beauty and find words inadequate to express it. A foolish student from the countryside, I wipe my eyes in eager expectation of it.

The Third Question

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
陳所蘊
同考試官教諭林　批　學術係于世重矣是作立意純正屬詞奇邁救弊補偏動中肯綮闗世教文字也
同考試官教諭汪　批　闡明學術而救弊振作之方鑿鑿可行必邃養之士
同考試官教諭鄧　批　古今學術之異剖析詳明是有裨世道者允宜于錄
同考試官教諭王　批　敷對詳明議論正大學術淵源足徵所自而經世事業亦可想見矣
===
敬服敬服
考試官右贊善陳　批　學術流弊敷陳甚悉而末以興起之術在振舉成法足為確論
考試官左中允戴　批　論興起學術而歸之養士用士亦有見
夫崇炳德業懋實學而翊昌期者純儒之芳軌也陶冶才賢敦化原而起末俗者明
王之大計也上古之士勵名重諸無窮學
punctuated:
陳所蘊

同考試官教諭林批：學術係于世重矣。是作立意純正，屬詞奇邁，救弊補偏，動中肯綮，闗世教文字也。
同考試官教諭汪批：闡明學術，而救弊振作之方，鑿鑿可行，必邃養之士。
同考試官教諭鄧批：古今學術之異，剖析詳明，是有裨世道者，允宜于錄。
同考試官教諭王批：敷對詳明，議論正大，學術淵源，足徵所自，而經世事業，亦可想見矣。敬服，敬服！
考試官右贊善陳批：學術流弊，敷陳甚悉，而末以興起之術在振舉成法，足為確論。
考試官左中允戴批：論興起學術，而歸之養士、用士，亦有見。

夫崇炳德業、懋實學而翊昌期者，純儒之芳軌也；陶冶才賢、敦化原而起末俗者，明王之大計也。上古之士，勵名重諸無窮，學
translation_en:
Chen Suoyun 陳所蘊

Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Lin comments: Scholarship bears heavily upon the world. This essay is pure and upright in conception, striking and lofty in diction. In remedying abuses and redressing imbalances, its every point hits the mark—a piece of writing of genuine consequence for the moral instruction of the age.
Associate Examiner Instructor Wang comments: It elucidates scholarship, and its methods for remedying abuses and rousing renewal are concrete and practicable; the author must be a scholar of deep cultivation.
Associate Examiner Instructor Deng comments: The differences between ancient and modern scholarship are analyzed in clear detail. As something beneficial to the moral order of the world, it truly deserves to be selected for record.
Associate Examiner Instructor Wang comments: The exposition and response are detailed and clear, and the arguments upright and grand. The origins and development of scholarship are sufficient to attest to his own grounding, and his capacity for statecraft can likewise be envisioned from this. Truly admirable, truly admirable!
Examiner Right Admonisher (you zanshan) Chen comments: The degenerate abuses of scholarship are set forth very thoroughly, and the conclusion that the way to revive it lies in invigorating established laws suffices as a sound judgment.
Examiner Left Companion (zuo zhongyun) Dai comments: In discussing the revival of scholarship and tracing it back to the nurturing and employment of scholars, he also shows insight.

Now, to exalt luminous virtue and achievement, strive after solid learning, and assist a flourishing era—this is the fragrant path of the pure Confucian scholar; to mold and refine men of talent and worth, thicken the wellsprings of transformation, and uplift decadent customs—this is the grand design of an enlightened ruler. The scholars of high antiquity strove after a reputation valued across endless generations, and their learning…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
皆究於實用其後士之所學非無以宏博
自號而皆未稱于古廼所謂敝焉耳則學
術者非上倡之不可矣不爲之倡而徒取
具于旦夕循襲于耳目以故爲士者枝葉
徒飾而本始之義虧蓄殖弗深而濟理之
誠塞卽圭組軒符日授于人何治安之有
邪是故豫養于未用者以示趨向之的也
精察于已用者以操鼓舞之機也率是以
往庶哉興起之一道矣夫學術所關于世
===
可不謂重哉書曰學于古訓乃有獲此傅
說訓高宗者言學不可已也第古人所爲
學大都與世學異焉闡明王伯剖晰義利
非以干祿也綜理丘索品藻名物非以循
象也俯仰賢聖嘉述上下非以炫博也綢
繆禮樂推合陰陽非以譁衆也矢陳謀猷
砥礪行業非以賈譽也上之以爲主寧邦
下之以拯民扶世內之潤帝猷而恢王議
外之過亂略而扞疆圉皆本諸身心而措
punctuated: 皆究於實用。其後士之所學，非無以宏博自號，而皆未稱于古，廼所謂敝焉耳。則學術者，非上倡之不可矣。不爲之倡，而徒取具于旦夕，循襲于耳目；以故爲士者，枝葉徒飾而本始之義虧，蓄殖弗深而濟理之誠塞，卽圭組軒符日授于人，何治安之有邪？是故豫養于未用者，以示趨向之的也；精察于已用者，以操鼓舞之機也。率是以往，庶哉興起之一道矣。夫學術所關于世，可不謂重哉！《書》曰：「學于古訓乃有獲。」此傅說訓高宗者，言學不可已也。第古人所爲學，大都與世學異焉：闡明王伯、剖晰義利，非以干祿也；綜理丘索、品藻名物，非以循象也；俯仰賢聖、嘉述上下，非以炫博也；綢繆禮樂、推合陰陽，非以譁衆也；矢陳謀猷、砥礪行業，非以賈譽也。上之以爲主寧邦，下之以拯民扶世，內之潤帝猷而恢王議，外之過亂略而扞疆圉，皆本諸身心而措
translation_en: … was all aimed at practical utility. Later on, what scholars studied did not lack claims to broad erudition, yet none of it matched antiquity; this is simply what is called decline. Thus, when it comes to scholarly learning, it will not do unless those above take the lead in promoting it. If one does not take the lead in promoting it, and instead merely seeks makeshifts for the immediate moment and follows routine conventions based on what meets the eye and ear, then those who are scholars will merely adorn the branches and leaves while the principles of the root and origin are impaired, and their cultivation and accumulation will not be deep while their sincere commitment to aiding and ordering the world is blocked. Even if jade tablets, official ribbons, high carriages, and tallies of authority are bestowed upon men every day, what peace and good order could there possibly be? Therefore, nurturing them beforehand prior to their employment is the way to point out the target toward which they should strive; examining them with precision after they have been employed is the way to grasp the mechanism for inspiring and rousing them. Proceeding along these lines, this should come close to being a way of revitalizing learning. Now, given how scholarly learning relates to the world, how could it not be called weighty! The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Study the ancient precepts, and then you will have attainment." This was Fu Yue instructing Gaozong, meaning that learning cannot be ceased. Yet what the ancients pursued as learning was on the whole different from the learning of the present age: they elucidated the ways of the true king and the hegemon and analyzed righteousness versus profit, not in order to seek official emoluments; they synthesized the Three Mounds and Eight Cords (Qiusuo) and appraised names and objects, not merely to follow outward appearances; they contemplated the worthies and sages and approvingly recounted matters high and low, not to show off broad erudition; they wove together rites and music and deduced the harmonies of yin and yang, not to dazzle the multitude; they set forth plans and counsels and honed their conduct and achievements, not to buy fame. Above, they used it to serve the ruler and bring tranquility to the state; below, to rescue the people and uphold the age; internally, to grace imperial counsels and expand kingly deliberations; externally, to check rebellious designs [?] and defend the frontiers—all of it was rooted in their own person and mind and put into…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
諸事業茲學之有裨于實用者邪昔伊尹
佐佑商王格于皇天不有調出于詩書者
乎其告太甲曰德無常師主善爲師信斯
言也則元聖之德非誦讀所能盡矣太公
作師襁褓表茲東海不有疑其爲陰謀者
乎其告武王曰敬勝者吉怠勝者滅信斯
言也則鷹揚之略非陰謀所可疑矣繇斯
以繹古人之學雖誦詩讀書不盡廢其所
業而不以偏才薄技特見其所長故學之
===
犖然獨著于世恒必繇之矣嗟乎士生三
代之後先王之教日以湮滅不存各就其
資之所近以爲學旣無所賴于上而上之
人又安其習尚不爲之所夫寡聞謏識無
論矣卽有振者其事功槩不免于議焉古
之實學蓋難言之矣姑以明問所及者而
評之公孫弘應詔賢良宜敷陳不媿于仲
舒矣乃假堯湯水旱之說以文其奸弘眞
曲學者哉谷永博通典籍宜直言不忝于
punctuated: 諸事業，茲學之有裨于實用者邪？昔伊尹佐佑商王，格于皇天，不有調出于《詩》、《書》者乎？其告太甲曰：「德無常師，主善爲師。」信斯言也，則元聖之德，非誦讀所能盡矣。太公作師襁褓，表茲東海，不有疑其爲陰謀者乎？其告武王曰：「敬勝者吉，怠勝者滅。」信斯言也，則鷹揚之略，非陰謀所可疑矣。繇斯以繹古人之學，雖誦《詩》讀《書》不盡廢其所業，而不以偏才薄技特見其所長，故學之犖然獨著于世，恒必繇之矣。嗟乎！士生三代之後，先王之教日以湮滅不存，各就其資之所近以爲學。旣無所賴于上，而上之人又安其習尚，不爲之所。夫寡聞謏識無論矣，卽有振者，其事功槩不免于議焉。古之實學，蓋難言之矣。姑以明問所及者而評之：公孫弘應詔賢良，宜敷陳不媿于仲舒矣，乃假堯、湯水旱之說以文其奸，弘眞曲學者哉！谷永博通典籍，宜直言不忝于
translation_en:
…into practical undertakings—is this not how learning proves beneficial to practical use? In antiquity, when Yi Yin 伊尹 assisted the Shang king and reached up to August Heaven, were there not those who said [reading 謂 for 調?] his achievement came from the Odes (Shi) and the Documents (Shu)? Yet when he counselled Taijia 太甲, he said: "Virtue has no constant teacher; taking goodness as master is one's teacher." If we trust these words, then the virtue of the Great Sage could not be exhausted by mere recitation and reading. When Duke Tai 太公 served as Grand Preceptor to a ruler in swaddling clothes and stood out as a model by the Eastern Sea, were there not those who suspected him of secret scheming? Yet when he counselled King Wu 武王, he said: "He whose reverence prevails will meet with auspiciousness; he whose indolence prevails will perish." If we trust these words, then his eagle-soaring strategy is beyond any suspicion of secret scheming. If from this we trace out the learning of the ancients, although they did not entirely abandon the pursuit of reciting the Odes and reading the Documents, they did not display their strengths merely through one-sided talents or petty skills; therefore, when their learning stood out brilliantly and uniquely in the world, it was invariably by this path.

Alas! For scholars born after the Three Dynasties, the teachings of the former kings have day by day sunk into oblivion and ceased to exist, so that each pursues learning according to whatever lies closest to his natural endowments. Not only have they nothing to rely upon from those above, but those above are content with prevailing customs and make no provision to guide them. Those of scant hearing and shallow understanding need not even be discussed; yet even when someone rouses himself to action, his practical achievements are on the whole not exempt from criticism. The practical learning of antiquity is indeed difficult to speak of! Let me tentatively evaluate those mentioned in Your Reverence's question: Gongsun Hong 公孫弘 responded to the imperial summons for the Worthy and Excellent (xianliang), and in setting forth his views he ought not to have been ashamed before Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒; yet he borrowed the talk of floods under Yao 堯 and droughts under Tang 湯 to gloss over his duplicity—Hong was truly a man of crooked learning! Gu Yong 谷永 was broadly conversant with the canonical texts, and in speaking forthrightly he ought not to have disgraced…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
更生矣何諛王鳳申伯之忠以固其寵永
其竊位者哉桓榮敷奏經書致位少傅遇
亦偶矣輜車乘馬以會勉諸生稽古果若
是邪馬融典校秘書名震關西才誠博矣
教授生徒而後列女樂範物宜固爾耶博
極羣書楊雄之學優矣乃撰劇秦美新之
論則博聞强記秪以資獵華躡要之階乎
經術經世安石之論似矣迺倡三不足畏
之說則苦心力學特以濟强辨執拗之計
===
乎之數子者其在當時皆褎然稱文學之
士矣顧姦詐如弘阿諛如永卑瑣佞奢如
榮如融彼哉無以議爲也子雲以著述稱
奇荊國以才名出世似有過人者焉一則
明哲不能保身一則紛更徒以召亂總之
沉溺于詞章之習支離於聞見之偏視古
之實學者邈不相及矣是故品隲古今之
學以通於振作之治而學術有不可舉者
哉
punctuated: 更生矣，何諛王鳳「申伯之忠」以固其寵？永其竊位者哉！桓榮敷奏經書，致位少傅，遇亦偶矣，輜車乘馬以會勉諸生，稽古果若是邪？馬融典校秘書，名震關西，才誠博矣，教授生徒而後列女樂，範物宜固爾耶？博極羣書，楊雄之學優矣，乃撰《劇秦美新》之論，則博聞强記，秪以資獵華躡要之階乎？經術經世，安石之論似矣，迺倡「三不足畏」之說，則苦心力學，特以濟强辨執拗之計乎？之數子者，其在當時，皆褎然稱文學之士矣。顧姦詐如弘，阿諛如永，卑瑣佞奢如榮、如融，彼哉！無以議爲也。子雲以著述稱奇，荊國以才名出世，似有過人者焉；一則明哲不能保身，一則紛更徒以召亂。總之，沉溺于詞章之習，支離於聞見之偏，視古之實學者邈不相及矣。是故品隲古今之學，以通於振作之治，而學術有不可舉者哉！
translation_en:
…Gengsheng [Liu Xiang 劉向]; why then did he flatter Wang Feng 王鳳 as having "the loyalty of the Earl of Shen" (Shen Bo 申伯) in order to secure his own favor? Yong [Gu Yong 谷永] was truly one who usurped his position! Huan Rong 桓榮 expounded on the Classics and rose to the position of Junior Tutor (Shaofu), which was indeed a rare encounter with imperial favor; yet he displayed his carriages and horses before the assembled students to encourage them—is the study of antiquity really for such ends? Ma Rong 馬融 was in charge of collating texts in the Imperial Library, and his fame shook Guanxi; his talent was truly broad, yet while teaching his disciples in front, he arrayed female musicians behind the curtain—should one who serves as a model for others really act like this? Having read exhaustively through all books, the learning of Yang Xiong 楊雄 was superior indeed; yet he composed the essay Criticizing Qin and Praising Xin (Ju Qin mei Xin), so did his broad learning and retentive memory serve merely as a stepping stone to hunt for glory and tread in high office? Ordering the world through classical scholarship—Wang Anshi's 王安石 arguments seemed plausible; yet he championed the doctrine of the "Three Unworthies of Fear," so did his painstaking and diligent study serve only to aid his schemes of stubborn sophistry and obstinacy?

All of these several men were, in their own times, preeminently acclaimed as scholars of literature and learning. Yet as for those who were treacherous and deceitful like Hong [Gongsun Hong 公孫弘], sycophantic like Yong, or base, petty, flattering, and extravagant like Rong and Rong—such men as those are not even worth discussing! Ziyun [Yang Xiong] was celebrated as extraordinary for his writings, and the Duke of Jing (Jingguo, i.e., Wang Anshi) stood out in the world for his reputation of talent; they seemed to surpass others. Yet the one lacked the wisdom to preserve his own integrity and life, while the other's chaotic alterations merely invited disorder. In sum, they were mired in the habits of ornate composition or fragmented by partiality of learning and observation; compared to those of ancient times who possessed substantive learning, they were worlds apart and could not match them. Therefore, if we evaluate the learning of ancient and modern times so as to connect it with a governance of revitalization, how could matters of scholarly principle not be raised and examined?

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
明興以來崇尚儒治海內章縫之士類能學
務醇明乘時翼運更僕未易悉數愚竊聞
而景慕之非漢宋諸子不免訾議者可同
日語矣今
天子踐阼申飭學政頃復責貢舉之精禁援納
之濫冀得實學者用之
意義甚盛而議者尚惜其不盡如古焉則奚
以故哉今之士口誦而目睹固先聖遺訓
也視盈咫而趨引繩外亦與與然都也郎
===
與三代之英絜功比德何以讓焉而實不
盡然者愚伏思之矣六經之旨闡明于賢
聖孰非以資德業也乃譚經者藻飾章句
而不體會于身心尋行數墨以為工獵異
標奇以自炫特藉為進身干譽之途而舊
業且弁髦棄之矣雖上智類多興起然如
此者不盡無也夫士譬則射也必視正鵠
之設運其巧力審其括度乃可以撥弦而
激矢此由基所以百發皆中也今之士弗
punctuated:
明興以來，崇尚儒治，海內章縫之士，類能學務醇明，乘時翼運，更僕未易悉數。愚竊聞而景慕之，非漢、宋諸子不免訾議者可同日語矣。今
天子踐阼，申飭學政，頃復責貢舉之精，禁援納之濫，冀得實學者用之，意義甚盛。而議者尚惜其不盡如古焉，則奚以故哉？今之士，口誦而目睹，固先聖遺訓也；視盈咫而趨引繩，外亦與與然都也。郎與三代之英絜功比德，何以讓焉？而實不盡然者，愚伏思之矣。六經之旨，闡明于賢聖，孰非以資德業也？乃譚經者，藻飾章句而不體會于身心，尋行數墨以為工，獵異標奇以自炫，特藉為進身干譽之途，而舊業且弁髦棄之矣。雖上智類多興起，然如此者不盡無也。夫士譬則射也，必視正鵠之設，運其巧力，審其括度，乃可以撥弦而激矢，此由基所以百發皆中也。今之士，弗
translation_en:
Since the rise of our Ming dynasty, Confucian governance has been esteemed. Throughout the realm, scholars in ceremonial caps and robes have generally devoted themselves to pure and luminous learning, seizing the moment to assist the dynastic destiny—so many that one could not easily recount them all even after changing attending servants. In my humble ignorance, I have heard of them and admired them from afar; they cannot be spoken of in the same breath as those masters of the Han and Song who did not escape criticism. Now the Son of Heaven has ascended the throne and issued strict instructions regarding educational administration. Recently He has again demanded refinement in tribute and examination selections and prohibited abuses in the purchase of student status, hoping to obtain men of substantive learning for employment. The intention behind this is magnificent indeed. Yet critics still regret that scholars do not entirely match those of antiquity—why is this so?

The scholars of today recite with their mouths and behold with their eyes what are assuredly the bequeathed teachings of the former sages; looking no further than a foot ahead and walking as if along a taut cord, outwardly they are also poised and refined. Even [郎 -> 即?] if we were to measure their achievements and compare their virtue with the heroes of the Three Dynasties, why should they yield to them? Yet in reality it is not entirely so, and I have humbly pondered the reason. The meanings of the Six Classics were elucidated by the sages and worthies—which of them was not meant to nourish virtue and enterprise? Yet those who discuss the Classics embellish phrases and sentences without embodying them in their own persons and minds; they count lines and tally ink-marks as skill, and hunt for novelty and parade eccentricity to show off, merely using them as a path to advance themselves and seek fame, while casting aside their former studies like a useless cap of infancy. Although men of the highest wisdom generally rise above this, those who act in such a manner are not entirely absent. Now, a scholar may be compared to an archer: he must look at the placement of the target's center, exert his skill and strength, and examine the nock and measure before he can release the bowstring and speed the arrow—this was how Yang Youji hit the mark a hundred times out of a hundred shots. The scholars of today do not…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
審鵠者耳即投之弧矢能貫百步之外而
不爽乎待銓之士囿羅于科目孰非以供
任使也乃蒞官者馳騁臆見而鮮諳達于
世務尚通競進以為能生事邀功以眩俗
非眞有匡時定難之心而公家將傳舍視
之矣雖豪傑固多樹建然若此者亦無幾
也夫士譬則御也必明越燕之途識其山
川熟其風土乃可以嚮方而適國此造父
所以一日千里也今之士直寘行者耳即
===
授之駿乘能驅南北之途而不迷乎執事
以為溺浮詞而鮮實蹟者是矣是矣夫今
所與共治者即天下之人才而人才則關
乎學術學術之汙隆即人才盛衰以之人
才之盛衰即治化興替以之所繫非淺尠
者迺學術大較若斯矣非盛世事也愚竊
謂此士習之謬而浸尋不覺以至是則始
於行法者重失其意焉何也
國家稽古定制損益百王其養士用士之法
punctuated: 審鵠者耳，即投之弧矢，能貫百步之外而不爽乎？待銓之士，囿羅于科目，孰非以供任使也？乃蒞官者，馳騁臆見而鮮諳達于世務，尚通競進以為能，生事邀功以眩俗，非眞有匡時定難之心，而公家將傳舍視之矣。雖豪傑固多樹建，然若此者亦無幾也。夫士譬則御也，必明越、燕之途，識其山川，熟其風土，乃可以嚮方而適國，此造父所以一日千里也。今之士，直寘行者耳，即授之駿乘，能驅南北之途而不迷乎？執事以為溺浮詞而鮮實蹟者，是矣，是矣！夫今所與共治者，即天下之人才，而人才則關乎學術。學術之汙隆，即人才盛衰以之；人才之盛衰，即治化興替以之，所繫非淺尠者。迺學術大較若斯矣，非盛世事也。愚竊謂此士習之謬，而浸尋不覺以至是，則始於行法者重失其意焉。何也？國家稽古定制，損益百王，其養士、用士之法，
translation_en: … carefully examine the target. Even if one hands them a bow and arrows, could they pierce a mark beyond a hundred paces without erring? As for scholars awaiting appointment, gathered in through the examination categories, which of them is not meant to serve in official assignments? Yet when they take office, they give free rein to subjective opinions and rarely have a thorough grasp of worldly affairs. They prize opportunism and compete for advancement as signs of ability, and they stir up trouble and court merit to dazzle the vulgar. They do not truly possess the heart to rectify the times and settle difficulties, and they come to regard the public realm as nothing more than a post-station inn. Although outstanding figures certainly achieve much, there are not many who are exempt from such faults. Now, a scholar may be compared to a charioteer: he must understand the roads to Yue and Yan, know their mountains and rivers, and be familiar with their local conditions before he can face the right direction and reach the destination. This was how Zaofu was able to cover a thousand li in a single day. Today's scholars are merely groping their way in the dark [寘 for 冥]; even if one grants them a team of fine steeds, could they drive along the roads north and south without losing their way? When Your Excellency deems that they are steeped in empty verbiage and rarely show substantive achievements, that is indeed so, indeed so! Now, those with whom the realm is governed today are none other than the talents of the world, and talent depends upon scholarship. The decline or flourishing of scholarship determines the waxing or waning of talent; the waxing or waning of talent determines the rise or fall of governance and moral transformation—what hinges upon this is by no means slight. Yet the general state of scholarship is like this, which is not a matter befitting a flourishing age. I humbly venture to say that this is an error in the literati ethos, and that its gradual, unperceived progression to this point began with those who administer the laws gravely losing sight of their original intent. Why is this? When the Dynasty examined antiquity to establish its institutions, adapting the ways of a hundred kings, its methods for nurturing and employing scholars…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
悉本虞周之意無以議爲矣顧今興起實
學之難者則學校選舉之間有以養之而
未預有以用之而未精也所云積漸之弊
致然者非耶夫古謂養士者非以給廩餼
絺章句已也將羣多士而涵育之俾其經
明德成以應有司之求也古謂用士者非
以積資序慎繩墨已也將弊羣材而責成
之俾其累伐績功以効敷施之實也今學
宮未嘗不設而養士之道漸微科目未嘗
===
不廣而用士之道漸失士之不能自勵于
學夫亦有自矣今因其敝而振作之則慎
師儒之選明本實之訓公辟薦之典覈考
課之蹟者所宜講也語曰峙高一丈築堵
八尺言人以模成也今士所督率非師長
乎學官多悋于羣居憲臣未悉其平日何
以示則也必擇堪師表者任之倡以德誼
不專于文詞勵以賞罰尤嚴于進退則師
道立而士所觀磨激發者衆矣杞梓之材
punctuated: 悉本虞、周之意，無以議爲矣。顧今興起實學之難者，則學校、選舉之間，有以養之而未預，有以用之而未精也。所云積漸之弊致然者，非耶？夫古謂養士者，非以給廩餼、絺章句已也，將羣多士而涵育之，俾其經明德成，以應有司之求也；古謂用士者，非以積資序、慎繩墨已也，將弊羣材而責成之，俾其累伐績功，以効敷施之實也。今學宮未嘗不設，而養士之道漸微；科目未嘗不廣，而用士之道漸失。士之不能自勵于學，夫亦有自矣！今因其敝而振作之，則慎師儒之選、明本實之訓、公辟薦之典、覈考課之蹟者，所宜講也。語曰：「峙高一丈，築堵八尺。」言人以模成也。今士所督率，非師長乎？學官多悋于羣居，憲臣未悉其平日，何以示則也？必擇堪師表者任之，倡以德誼，不專于文詞；勵以賞罰，尤嚴于進退。則師道立，而士所觀磨激發者衆矣。杞梓之材，
translation_en:
… are all based on the intentions of Yu [Shun] and the Zhou dynasty, leaving nothing to be criticized. Yet today, the difficulty in reviving practical learning lies in the fact that between the schools and the selection system, there are means to nurture scholars, yet without foresight; and there are means to employ them, yet without refinement. Is this not what is meant by cumulative and gradual abuses bringing things to such a pass?

What the ancients called nurturing scholars was not merely providing stipends of grain and weaving together chapters and sentences; rather, it was gathering the multitude of scholars and nurturing them so that their mastery of the Classics would be clear and their virtue perfected, in order to meet the demands of the authorities. What the ancients called employing scholars was not merely accumulating seniority and cautiously adhering to rules and regulations; rather, it was evaluating [弊, read as 幣/弊=斷/定] all talents and holding them responsible for results, so that they would accumulate merit and achievement to deliver the reality of effective governance. Nowadays, state schools have not failed to be established, yet the way of nurturing scholars has gradually declined; the examination categories have not failed to be broad, yet the way of employing scholars has gradually been lost. That scholars cannot rouse themselves to learning truly has its source!

If today, in view of these defects, we wish to invigorate them, then carefully selecting teachers and Confucian instructors, clarifying teachings of fundamental substance, making impartial the statutes of recruitment and recommendation, and verifying the actual achievements in personnel evaluations are what ought to be discussed. The proverb says: "To pile a mound ten feet high, one builds an eight-foot wall [as a mold]"—meaning that men are formed through a model. Now, are not those who supervise and lead the scholars their teachers and elders? Yet educational officials are often remiss when living among the students, and the Censorial Officials do not fully know their everyday conduct—how then can they set a standard? We must select those worthy of being paragons for teachers and appoint them, leading through moral rectitude rather than focusing solely on literary composition, and encouraging through rewards and punishments while being especially strict regarding advancement and dismissal. Then the way of the teacher will be established, and the scholars who observe, polish one another, and are inspired will be many.

As for timber of catalytic willow and catalpa…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
匠氏操引顧之以其具足棟明堂耳士執
空文而草略登仕最大患也則課以經術
必校其躬行習以世務必求其實用如胡
瑗經義治事者後官書其績歲考其成庶
異日所使卽今日所教而學皆可用矣十
步之內必有豐草所求貴愽也環宇內之
大豈無一二潛心大業如古人者乎令所
司稽實疏名以聞眞爲特異之學問一薦
拔之而冐濫者有罰此風士勵俗之助亦
===
先朝故事也吹竽滿庭一一聽之乃識其音耳
士不核治行詎則信之如錢穀甲兵法律
河渠必各擇材器所宜以授之職而久任
責成之徐察其治理何若果稽古準今積
有成効必幹濟之學講籌平日者至熟也
夫數者皆法所已試往者得士之効罔不
繇此第沿襲旣久視爲故說迂圖漫不加
意而爲士者亦狃習于俗之所趨以故下
不得其養而上亦不得其用學術所以不
punctuated: 匠氏操引顧之，以其具足棟明堂耳。士執空文而草略登仕，最大患也。則課以經術，必校其躬行；習以世務，必求其實用。如胡瑗經義、治事者，後官書其績，歲考其成，庶異日所使，卽今日所教，而學皆可用矣。十步之內，必有豐草，所求貴愽也。環宇內之大，豈無一二潛心大業如古人者乎？令所司稽實疏名以聞，眞爲特異之學，問一薦拔之，而冐濫者有罰，此風士勵俗之助，亦先朝故事也。吹竽滿庭，一一聽之，乃識其音耳。士不核治行，詎則信之？如錢穀、甲兵、法律、河渠，必各擇材器所宜以授之職，而久任責成之，徐察其治理何若。果稽古準今，積有成効，必幹濟之學講籌平日者至熟也。夫數者，皆法所已試，往者得士之効，罔不繇此。第沿襲旣久，視爲故說迂圖，漫不加意，而爲士者亦狃習于俗之所趨。以故下不得其養，而上亦不得其用，學術所以不
translation_en: … the master carpenter holds his plumb line and looks upon it with favor, simply because its timber is sufficient to serve as a ridgepole for the Hall of Light (Mingtang). For scholars to cling to empty words and carelessly ascend into officialdom is the greatest of evils. Therefore, when testing them in classical statecraft, we must examine their personal conduct; when training them in worldly affairs, we must demand practical utility. As with Hu Yuan's 胡瑗 divisions of "Classical Meaning" (jingyi) and "Administrative Affairs" (zhishi), let their subsequent offices record their achievements and annually evaluate their results. In this way, what they are employed to do in the future will be precisely what they are taught today, and their learning will all be applicable for use. Within ten paces there is surely abundant grass; what matters in seeking is breadth. Throughout the vastness of the empire, how could there not be one or two men who devote their minds to the great enterprise like the ancients? Let the competent authorities verify the facts and submit their names in a memorial to the throne; if theirs is truly learning of extraordinary distinction, occasionally recommend and promote them, while punishing those who make fraudulent or excessive claims. This is an aid to inspiring scholars and encouraging customs, and is also a precedent from former reigns. When reed-organ players fill the courtyard, only by listening to them one by one can one discern their musical skill. If scholars are not verified by their administrative performance, how can they be trusted? In matters such as revenue and grain, armor and weaponry, laws and statutes, and rivers and canals, we must select men according to the suitability of their talents and capacities, confer offices upon them, keep them in long-term appointments while holding them responsible for results, and unhurriedly observe how their governance turns out. If indeed they examine antiquity and adapt to the present, accumulating proven efficacy, it must be that their learning in practical statecraft was discussed and planned for with the utmost familiarity in ordinary times. Now, these several measures are all methods that have already been tested; in the past, the efficacy of obtaining capable scholars invariably derived from them. Yet because they have been routinely followed for so long, people regard them as stale talk and impractical schemes, paying them no heed at all, while those who are scholars also grow accustomed to following vulgar trends. Consequently, those below do not receive proper nurturing, and those above do not obtain their practical use; this is why scholarship fails to…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
及于古也茲不必更易成法取所已試者
振舉于上務求實効使培植有方不才者
不得倖進綜覈有法倖進者不得苟容積
之數年養士用士之中默寓鼓之飭之之
術
意嚮所及風行海流士皆知無實之學不足
以待用將必以浮詞爲愧而茂蹟是期所
謂實學之士亦庶乎可拔十得五矣興學
造士莢無出此者雖然振厲學術機在上
也其自振于學者事在士也故曰豪傑之
===
士雖無文王猶興況
聖人在上教化大明之日愚生甄陶樂育可謂
厚幸矣上知養士而士不知自養上知用
士而士不知自用固執事所耻而愚生竊
鄙者也
第四問
程懋德
同考試官教諭伍 批〔吏治有裨於世以黜〕
punctuated:
及于古也。茲不必更易成法，取所已試者振舉于上，務求實効，使培植有方，不才者不得倖進；綜覈有法，倖進者不得苟容。積之數年，養士、用士之中，默寓鼓之、飭之之術。意嚮所及，風行海流，士皆知無實之學不足以待用，將必以浮詞爲愧而茂蹟是期，所謂實學之士，亦庶乎可拔十得五矣！興學造士，莢無出此者。雖然，振厲學術，機在上也；其自振于學者，事在士也。故曰：「豪傑之士，雖無文王猶興。」況聖人在上，教化大明之日，愚生甄陶樂育，可謂厚幸矣！上知養士而士不知自養，上知用士而士不知自用，固執事所耻，而愚生竊鄙者也。

第四問
程懋德
同考試官教諭伍 批〔吏治有裨於世，以黜〕
translation_en:
… match antiquity. Today there is no need to alter the established laws; rather, those above should take what has already been tested and vigorously put it into practice, striving for actual results. Ensure that there is a proper method for nurturing talent, so that the untalented cannot advance by luck; and ensure that there is a system for comprehensive verification, so that those who have advanced by luck cannot idly remain in office. Over the course of several years, within the processes of nurturing and employing scholars, the techniques of encouraging and disciplining them will be quietly embedded. As the ruler's intentions reach outward, spreading like the wind and flowing like the sea, scholars will all know that learning devoid of substance is insufficient to await employment. They will surely come to feel ashamed of empty verbiage and instead aspire to splendid achievements; thus, among the so-called scholars of solid learning, we may perhaps select ten and obtain five! For reviving learning and cultivating scholars, there is no plan [莢, OCR for 策] that surpasses this. Even so, the pivot for invigorating scholarly learning lies with those above, whereas the task of rousing oneself in learning lies with the scholars themselves. Therefore it is said: "Outstanding scholars rise up even without a King Wen." How much more so in an age when a Sage is on the throne and moral transformation shines brilliantly! For a foolish student like myself to be molded and joyfully nurtured may truly be called a great fortune. If those above know how to nurture scholars, yet scholars do not know how to nurture themselves; if those above know how to employ scholars, yet scholars do not know how to make themselves useful—this is surely what Your Excellency considers shameful, and what I, a foolish student, privately despise.

Fourth Question
Cheng Maode 程懋德
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Wu 伍: [For administrative governance to benefit the world, it is a matter of dismissing …]

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
虛名崇實效耳子獨能闡發而復以辨析之責
歸諸上是常留心於天下者宜錄以式
考試官右贊善陳　批〔吏治不飭以眩於名實也子指陳弊端歷歷明甚且區畫精詳議論剴切〕
他日爲實用之士可預占矣
考試官左中允戴　批〔辨名實以正士習而飭吏治此當今切要之論子敷對確然可行必書生〕
而負經世之略者錄之
===
今天下有勢焉是時所共趨而治之繇敝
也欲振吏治之敝非因勢以輕重之不可
矣夫治之始也無有不盛而行之既久或
至于敝則世襲泰寧瑕纇潛長人心怠弛
名實失眞勢必至此也勢之所在時競趨
之而經世者務一切因循曰吾以鎭俗而
養量將敝且日甚釀爲大患必察天下之
勢辨名實以挽之則治之所倡時之耳目
化焉風之所劑世之習尚移焉上以實辨
下下以實應上而振作吏治之良筴當不
punctuated:
虛名、崇實效耳。子獨能闡發，而復以辨析之責歸諸上，是常留心於天下者，宜錄以式。
考試官右贊善陳批：〔吏治不飭，以眩於名實也。子指陳弊端，歷歷明甚，且區畫精詳，議論剴切，〕他日爲實用之士，可預占矣。
考試官左中允戴批：〔辨名實以正士習而飭吏治，此當今切要之論。子敷對確然可行，必書生〕而負經世之略者，錄之。
今天下有勢焉，是時所共趨而治之繇敝也。欲振吏治之敝，非因勢以輕重之不可矣。夫治之始也，無有不盛，而行之既久，或至于敝，則世襲泰寧，瑕纇潛長，人心怠弛，名實失眞，勢必至此也。勢之所在，時競趨之，而經世者務一切因循，曰：「吾以鎭俗而養量。」將敝且日甚，釀爲大患。必察天下之勢，辨名實以挽之，則治之所倡，時之耳目化焉；風之所劑，世之習尚移焉。上以實辨下，下以實應上，而振作吏治之良筴，當不
translation_en:
… empty reputation and exalting tangible results. You alone are able to elucidate this, and moreover attribute the responsibility for discerning and analyzing it to those above. This shows that you constantly keep the empire in mind; your essay should be recorded as a model.

Examiner Chen, Right Admonisher (you zanshan), comments: 〔Official administration is not in good order because people are confused about reputation and reality. You point out and set forth the abuses, item by item, with great clarity; moreover, your planning is precise and detailed, and your arguments are incisive and to the point.〕 That you will one day be a scholar of practical use can already be foretold.

Examiner Dai, Left Companion (zuo zhongyun), comments: 〔Discerning reputation and reality in order to rectify the habits of scholars and put official administration in order—this is a discourse of urgent importance for the present day. Your exposition and reply are soundly practicable; you must be a scholar〕 who possesses strategies for ordering the world. Record it.

In the empire today there is a prevailing tendency: it is that toward which the age collectively gravitates, and the reason why governance falls into decay. If one wishes to revive official administration from its decay, one cannot do so without adjusting the relative weight of things in accordance with this tendency. Now at the beginning of a regime's governance, there is none that is not flourishing; yet when it has been practiced for a long time, it sometimes reaches the point of decay. For when successive generations inherit peace and tranquility, flaws and blemishes secretly grow, people's minds become lax and slack, and reputation and reality lose their truth—the tendency inevitably comes to this. Where the tendency lies, the age competes to follow it; yet those who manage the world devote themselves entirely to routine and passivity, saying: "By this I calm popular customs and cultivate magnanimity." Thus the decay will grow worse by the day and brew into a great disaster. One must examine the tendency of the empire and discern reputation and reality in order to reverse it; then, through what governance initiates, the eyes and ears of the age will be transformed, and through what the prevailing wind tempers, the customs and fashions of the world will shift. Those above will discern those below by means of reality, and those below will respond to those above by means of reality; the best policy for invigorating official administration surely does not…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
外是矣執事慨吏治日媮而以名實之辨
下詢末學此憂世之盛心也愚生有激于
衷久矣竊觀古今之議每不取務名之士
而論治者類以抑浮名崇實效爲言此何
以故哉蓋實者名之主名者實之賔實立
而名從之未有亡其實而徒享其名者也
故天下之患莫大於名實之不相蒙此先
實後名固上世之令圖而循名責實尤救
時之要論矣昔唐虞三代之閒非所稱明
===
盛之朝乎君以實德在上而五臣十二牧
九官十人又師師濟濟披心腹而貢忠誠
一以純然無僞之心注爲實政樹爲實功
以故皇澤豐霈宇內安瀾今睹詩書所稱
曰百工惟時撫于五辰曰疏附後先奔走
禦侮是上世郅隆之業所藉于數臣之力
非鮮淺矣自茲以往上鮮躬行之德下亡
精白之誠始亦小康而卒尋于亂漢去古
未遠唐猶近漢虛名爲害大氐已然而責
punctuated: 外是矣。執事慨吏治日媮，而以名實之辨下詢末學，此憂世之盛心也，愚生有激于衷久矣。竊觀古今之議，每不取務名之士，而論治者類以抑浮名、崇實效爲言，此何以故哉？蓋實者名之主，名者實之賔；實立而名從之，未有亡其實而徒享其名者也。故天下之患，莫大於名實之不相蒙。此先實後名，固上世之令圖；而循名責實，尤救時之要論矣。昔唐、虞、三代之閒，非所稱明盛之朝乎？君以實德在上，而五臣、十二牧、九官、十人，又師師濟濟，披心腹而貢忠誠，一以純然無僞之心，注爲實政，樹爲實功。以故皇澤豐霈，宇內安瀾。今睹《詩》、《書》所稱，曰：「百工惟時，撫于五辰。」曰：「疏附後先，奔走禦侮。」是上世郅隆之業，所藉于數臣之力，非鮮淺矣。自茲以往，上鮮躬行之德，下亡精白之誠，始亦小康，而卒尋于亂。漢去古未遠，唐猶近漢，虛名爲害，大氐已然，而責…
translation_en:
… beyond this. You, sir, lamenting that administrative governance grows daily more remiss, have condescended to ask a humble student about the distinction between reputation and reality. This shows an abundant heart that worries for the world, and I, a foolish student, have long been stirred by this within my breast.

Humbly observing discussions past and present, they consistently disapprove of scholars who pursue mere reputation, while those who discourse on governance generally speak of suppressing empty fame and exalting substantive results. Why is this so? Because reality is the master of reputation, and reputation is the guest of reality; when reality is established, reputation follows it, and there has never been anyone who lost the reality yet enjoyed the reputation in vain. Therefore, among the afflictions of the realm, none is greater than reputation and reality failing to correspond to one another. Thus, putting reality first and reputation second was indeed the fine plan of high antiquity, while demanding reality in accordance with reputation is especially the essential argument for rescuing the present age.

In ancient times, during the eras of Tang [Yao], Yu [Shun], and the Three Dynasties, were those not what we call enlightened and flourishing dynasties? The ruler occupied the throne with substantive virtue, while the Five Ministers, the Twelve Pastors, the Nine Officials, and the Ten Worthies, all in harmonious and dignified multitude, laid bare their hearts and offered up their loyal sincerity. Entirely with pure and unfeigned minds, they channeled this into substantive governance and established substantive achievements. For this reason, imperial beneficence flowed abundantly, and all within the world was calm and peaceful. Today, when we look at what is praised in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing) and the Classic of History (Shujing), one says: "All the officials are timely and follow the five seasonal cycles"; and the other says: "Some drew the estranged closer, some attended before and behind, some hastened in service, and some warded off insult." Thus, the supremely prosperous enterprise of high antiquity owed no small debt to the strength of those several ministers.

From that time onward, superiors rarely possessed the virtue of personal practice, and inferiors lost the sincerity of pure integrity; although there was minor prosperity at first, it eventually ended in disorder. The Han was not yet far removed from antiquity, and the Tang was still close to the Han, yet the harm done by empty reputation was in general already so, and the … [demanding of reality] …

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
實之說紛然矣宋以忠厚立國法制議論
似非二代所及而國勢愈弱人心多變積
弊之久君臣思建議倡之志何偉也迄不
逮焉蓋法制太勝而愈滋奸僞之風議論
徒多而無救積衰之勢當時崇實之論司
馬光胡寅巳諄諄言之故終宋之世而成
功少也名實不核難以善治前事可徵矣
此可不辨耶
明興以來
===
列聖相承政教大備度越千古今熙平餘二百
年矣愚生跧伏草野甞覽睹
國史所紀述見洪武永樂間法令尚嚴居官
者日惟惴惴奉法守職總之顧淸議而重
公家務正直而耻浮薄爭以行業相高聲
與華未露也是時上以實求而下以實應
故一時政善民殷吏治炳炳然盛焉入弘
正嘉隆之季習凡幾變其間策勛竪名之
士固多照耀于世然長老則喁喁爭言
punctuated: 實之說紛然矣。宋以忠厚立國，法制議論，似非二代所及，而國勢愈弱，人心多變。積弊之久，君臣思建議倡之，志何偉也！迄不逮焉。蓋法制太勝，而愈滋奸僞之風；議論徒多，而無救積衰之勢。當時崇實之論，司馬光、胡寅巳諄諄言之，故終宋之世而成功少也。名實不核，難以善治，前事可徵矣，此可不辨耶？明興以來，列聖相承，政教大備，度越千古，今熙平餘二百年矣。愚生跧伏草野，甞覽睹國史所紀述，見洪武、永樂間法令尚嚴，居官者日惟惴惴奉法守職。總之，顧淸議而重公家，務正直而耻浮薄，爭以行業相高，聲與華未露也。是時上以實求，而下以實應，故一時政善民殷，吏治炳炳然盛焉。入弘、正、嘉、隆之季，習凡幾變，其間策勛竪名之士，固多照耀于世，然長老則喁喁爭言
translation_en:
… Holding performance accountable to reality arose in profusion. The Song founded its state upon loyalty and generosity; its legal institutions and policy deliberations seemed beyond what those two previous dynasties had achieved, yet the strength of the state grew ever weaker and people's minds grew ever more fickle. After abuses had accumulated for a long time, ruler and ministers sought to offer proposals and initiate reforms—how grand were their ambitions! Yet in the end they fell short. This was because legal regulations were overly elaborate, which only further fostered a climate of deceit and fraud; and deliberations were merely numerous, doing nothing to rescue the dynasty from its accumulated decline. At the time, Sima Guang 司馬光 and Hu Yin 胡寅 already spoke earnestly in their discourses on esteeming reality, and thus throughout the entire Song dynasty actual achievements were few. When name and reality are not verified against each other, it is difficult to achieve good governance—past events verify this! How can one fail to discern this?

Since the rise of the Ming, successive Emperors have carried on the heritage; governance and moral instruction have been grandly perfected, surpassing all antiquity, and now peace and prosperity have lasted for more than two hundred years. Crouching in the rustic wilds, I, a foolish student, have had occasion to read what is recorded in the dynasty's histories, and have seen that during the Hongwu (1368–1398) and Yongle (1403–1424) eras, laws and ordinances were still strict, and those who held office spent their days in anxious fear, obeying the law and keeping to their duties. In short, they heeded pure criticism and valued the public interest, strove for uprightness and were ashamed of frivolity, and vied to excel one another in conduct and achievement, while empty reputation and ostentation had not yet appeared. At that time, those above sought with reality, and those below responded with reality; therefore, for an era governance was good and the people were prosperous, and official administration flourished brilliantly. Entering the later periods of the Hongzhi (1488–1505), Zhengde (1506–1521), Jiajing (1522–1566), and Longqing (1567–1572) eras, customs have changed several times. Among them, gentlemen who established merit and erected reputations have indeed often shone brightly in the world, yet the elders eagerly vie to speak of…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
國初時矣非以承平日久而實有不足則然
與何也一代之初天造草昧風氣返朴而
還淳人心直實而畏法聲容弗侈茂樸未
漓天下之事日入于實渢渢乎古風已迨
其久也浸尋以滋于敝則承襲熙恬羣情
懈弛之故識者之所竊憂非有槪于此邪
姑舉往事一二言之有司約巳愛民者固
衆矣而其間務甘言以巧宦術飭初政以
希薦剡亦不爲少焉甚至谿壑可盈印綬
===
冠不愧矣而徒據文飾以爲殿最何以精
考核也賦有常額而費多出于無經加以
私囊之乾沒豪猾之蠶食故所在蕭條矣
有司又取盈焉民柰何不窮且盜也縉紳
之士務爲容飾習爲選耎案積牘朽官不
能稽而巧僞百出矣此何以劾靖共塞奸
竇也讞獄有
詔而拘成牒者憚於改駁涉隱情者畏於詳
鞫往往糾察細過而廋巨蠹非詰慝之要
punctuated: 國初時矣。非以承平日久，而實有不足則然與？何也？一代之初，天造草昧，風氣返朴而還淳，人心直實而畏法，聲容弗侈，茂樸未漓，天下之事日入于實，渢渢乎古風已。迨其久也，浸尋以滋于敝，則承襲熙恬、羣情懈弛之故。識者之所竊憂，非有槪于此邪？姑舉往事一二言之：有司約巳愛民者固衆矣，而其間務甘言以巧宦術、飭初政以希薦剡，亦不爲少焉。甚至谿壑可盈，印綬冠不愧矣，而徒據文飾以爲殿最，何以精考核也？賦有常額，而費多出于無經，加以私囊之乾沒、豪猾之蠶食，故所在蕭條矣，有司又取盈焉，民柰何不窮且盜也？縉紳之士，務爲容飾，習爲選耎，案積牘朽，官不能稽，而巧僞百出矣，此何以劾靖共、塞奸竇也？讞獄有詔，而拘成牒者憚於改駁，涉隱情者畏於詳鞫，往往糾察細過而廋巨蠹，非詰慝之要
translation_en:
… the beginning of the dynasty. Is it not that because peace has lasted for so long, substance has grown deficient, thus making things so? Why is this? At the founding of an era, when Heaven creates out of rough obscurity, the prevailing ethos returns to simplicity and reverts to purity; people's hearts are straightforward, honest, and law-abiding; outward reputations and appearances are not extravagant, and lush simplicity has not yet been watered down. The affairs of the empire daily enter into genuine substance—grandly indeed, in the manner of antiquity! When a long time has passed, things gradually deteriorate into abuses, which is the result of inheriting peace and ease and of general sentiments growing lax. What men of insight secretly worry about—is it not precisely because they are moved by this?

Let me tentatively cite one or two past matters to speak of it. Among local authorities, those who restrain themselves and cherish the people are certainly numerous; yet among them, those who strive after sweet words in order to be clever in the art of officialdom, or who dress up their initial administration in hopes of recommendations, are also not few. It even reaches the point where their bottomless greed can be filled, and they feel no shame before their official seals, ribbons, and caps [?]; yet if one merely relies on superficial embellishments to determine the lowest and highest merit ratings, how can performance evaluations be made precise? Taxes have regular quotas, yet expenditures mostly arise from unregulated sources; added to this are the embezzlement into private pockets and the piecemeal devouring by powerful and cunning scoundrels. Thus everywhere is desolate and bleak, and when the authorities still demand the full surplus, how can the people not be driven to destitution and banditry? Gentlemen of the officialdom strive for outward ornament and grow accustomed to timidity and weakness; case files pile up and documents rot without officials being able to audit them, so that clever frauds emerge in a hundred ways. How by this means can one achieve quiet devotion to duty and block up the holes of villainy? For the adjudication of criminal cases there are imperial decrees, yet those bound by established dossiers shrink from revising or refuting them, and those dealing with hidden circumstances fear conducting thorough interrogations; time and again they censure minor faults while concealing giant parasites, which is not the essential way to investigate evil…

title: 萬曆四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也議事者工詞說而不察
成憲據臆見而弗持大體
制令始出譁然盈庭即
轂下爾爾矣此輕亵替而玩
詔令也其佗名存實亡當不止此皆曩者吏
治之弊也豈一朝夕之故哉語云琴瑟不
調更張乃鼓是之謂矣今
上銳意隆古深燭弊源去文崇實屢廑
聖諭端揆之臣恭寅以倡之非
===
明良一時者哉顧中令雖勤實効罔獲論者謂
玩愒之久世恬然安之而猝與更始猶移
江河而行之山也嗟乎此不然矣董子曰
下之從上如泥在器惟甄所爲如金在鎔
惟冶所鑄真善喻也今
上有求治之君而下無咸熙之績內有承式之
臣而外無允釐之効咎將誰執邪愚以爲
寔今士大夫之責試觀今日之域中方宇
寧謐無賦車籍馬之警也品式具備有運
punctuated: 也。議事者工詞說而不察成憲，據臆見而弗持大體，制令始出，譁然盈庭，即轂下爾爾矣。此輕亵替而玩詔令也。其佗名存實亡，當不止此，皆曩者吏治之弊也，豈一朝夕之故哉？語云：「琴瑟不調，更張乃鼓。」是之謂矣。今上銳意隆古，深燭弊源，去文崇實，屢廑聖諭，端揆之臣恭寅以倡之，非明良一時者哉？顧中令雖勤，實効罔獲。論者謂玩愒之久，世恬然安之，而猝與更始，猶移江河而行之山也。嗟乎！此不然矣。董子曰：「下之從上，如泥在器，惟甄所爲；如金在鎔，惟冶所鑄。」真善喻也！今上有求治之君，而下無咸熙之績；內有承式之臣，而外無允釐之効，咎將誰執邪？愚以爲寔今士大夫之責。試觀今日之域中，方宇寧謐，無賦車籍馬之警也；品式具備，有運
translation_en:
… [essential point of eradicating evil]. Those who deliberate on state affairs are skillful with rhetoric without examining the established statutes; they rely on subjective opinions without upholding the broad principles of governance. No sooner is an imperial command issued than a clamor fills the court—even right beneath the Sovereign's chariot [in the capital] it is like this! This is treating imperial authority with disrespect and trifling with imperial decrees [?]. Other instances where the name remains but the reality is lost surely do not stop at these. All are the abuses of past administrative governance; how could they have come about in a single morning or evening? As the saying goes: "When the qin and se zithers are out of tune, one must unstring and restring them before playing." This is precisely what is meant.

Now the reigning Emperor sets His mind keenly on theflourishing antiquity, deeply illuminates the sources of abuse, discards empty form to venerate substance, and repeatedly issues Sacred Edicts with earnest concern, while the chief ministers at the head of the administration respectfully and reverently take the lead—is this not an age when an enlightened ruler and virtuous ministers meet as one? Yet although ordinances from the court are frequent and diligent, substantive results are not achieved. Commentators say that after a long period of laxity and neglect, the world rests complacently in it, and that to abruptly initiate renewal with them is like trying to divert rivers and streams to flow over mountains. Alas, this is not so! Master Dong [Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒] said: "Subordinates follow superiors like clay on the wheel, shaped solely as the potter makes it; or like metal in the crucible, cast solely as the founder molds it." Truly an apt metaphor! Now above there is a ruler who seeks good governance, yet below there is no achievement of universal prosperity; within the court there are ministers who uphold the model, yet outside in the provinces there is no effect of sincere regulation. Who then shall bear the blame? In my humble view, it is truly the responsibility of today's scholar-officials.
